mechanisms.name: Status quo: anonymous public-read GCS bucket, publisher pays egress (gnomAD's own VCF downloads work this way)
mechanisms.what: Immutable, hash-pinned objects on a public bucket that anyone can fetch over HTTPS with no account. This is what genomeOS does today (genomeos-atlas-data plus genomeos-atlas-web, scripts/fetch_data.py using only the standard library). gnomAD works the same way for its VCFs: 'We pay for each VCF download of our data.'
mechanisms.userFriction: None. A URL or a standard-library script. No account, key or card.
mechanisms.costToUs: GCS internet egress is $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB a month, $0.11/GiB for 10-150 TiB and $0.08/GiB above that (worldwide excluding Asia and Australia; China $0.23, Australia $0.19). Always Free gives 100 GB a month of egress from North America, but only for buckets in us-west1, us-central1 or us-east1. Class B reads cost $0.0004 per 1,000. At $0.12/GiB, the $200 budget covers about 1.6 TiB a month. Current artifacts are MB-scale (the HbS surface is 1.1 MB), so today's data costs almost nothing to serve. The risk is volume from future raw harvests and models.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No. The publisher pays every byte. The existing kill switch at 150% of budget is the only backstop, and it takes the data offline.
mechanisms.ops: Already built and minimal: budget alerts, the kill switch, no-overwrite publishing.
mechanisms.limits: Uncapped liability for a viral or scripted download. gnomAD's July 2020 notice says the project was 'billed thousands of dollars in cloud egress charges' in a single month, mostly from users reading its US bucket from other regions. It then moved its Hail tables to Requester Pays.

mechanisms.name: gnomAD multi-cloud public-dataset hosting (Google Cloud Public Datasets + AWS Registry of Open Data)
mechanisms.what: gnomAD's Data page says data is 'available for download through Google Cloud Public Datasets, and the Registry of Open Data on AWS' (gs://gcp-public-data--gnomad, s3://gnomad-public-us-east-1). Azure Open Datasets access ended on 15 August 2025 when Microsoft deprecated its genomic datasets. Google also hosts a BigQuery copy, which gnomAD says 'is maintained entirely by Google'. The browser's GraphQL API is public for small, low-latency lookups. Google's announcement says users get the data 'across all Google Cloud regions ... without paying egress charges' and that 1 TB a month of BigQuery processing is free. The AWS bucket is read anonymously (--no-sign-request).
mechanisms.userFriction: Bulk files: none. The AWS CLI or gsutil works anonymously. BigQuery: a Google account, using either the sandbox or a billing project.
mechanisms.costToUs: Close to $0 for gnomAD. Google's program pays storage, and AWS ODP pays storage and egress. gnomAD still pays for the browser and for VCF downloads from its own bucket.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 for files. BigQuery: 1 TiB a month free, then $6.25/TiB.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, by moving cost to cloud sponsors and to users' own query bills rather than by charging.
mechanisms.ops: Keep two or three mirrors in sync. Program onboarding (see the AWS ODP and Google programs below). The cloud providers can drop a dataset, as Azure did in 2025.
mechanisms.limits: Sponsorship is at the provider's discretion and can end. AWS ODP needs open licences. gnomAD gives no support for the Google-maintained BigQuery copy.

mechanisms.name: AWS Open Data Sponsorship Program (ODP) and Registry of Open Data (RODA)
mechanisms.what: The FAQ says ODP covers 'Amazon S3 storage costs for the specific dataset approved under the program, as well as distribution costs such as egress and cross-region data fees'. Compute and analytics are not covered. RODA is the catalog. A dataset can be listed on RODA without sponsorship, in which case the owner pays. Applications are judged on accessibility (well documented, openly licensed, non-proprietary formats), cloud readiness, community engagement and demand, on a rolling basis, with a decision in about two weeks. Accepted datasets need a YAML registry entry by GitHub PR, documentation, a tutorial notebook, a new AWS account used only for hosting, and a bucket built from AWS's CloudFormation template. On renewal, the Open Data team reviews usage metrics. OpenAlex uses ODP for its free snapshot: ODP 'covers the data-transfer fees (about $70 per download)', and no AWS account is needed.
mechanisms.userFriction: None. Anonymous S3 (--no-sign-request) or HTTPS.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 for storage and egress of the sponsored dataset. Our cost is the one-off onboarding work and a dedicated AWS account.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes. AWS absorbs the cost, so there is nothing to recover.
mechanisms.ops: Application, an AWS account only for hosting, a sync job from the GCS source of truth to S3, a tutorial notebook, and a usage review at renewal.
mechanisms.limits: Data must be 'open to everyone and usable for any purpose at no cost'. CC BY 4.0 is recommended. Licences that restrict commercial use, such as CC BY-NC, or that restrict modification are not permitted. Gated access is not allowed. So fields genomeOS marks non_commercial or restricted (genomeos/publication/commercial_use.py lists gnomad.spliceai and alphagenome.top_attributions) cannot ship to an ODP mirror. A paid or login tier cannot live there either. Sponsorship is reviewed at renewal.

mechanisms.name: Google Cloud Public Datasets Program plus the BigQuery sandbox
mechanisms.what: Google says 'Google pays for the storage of these datasets and provides public access to the data using a project'. Users pay only for their queries, and 'The first 1 TB per month is free'. Users can 'start querying public datasets without enabling billing'. The BigQuery sandbox needs no credit card or billing account. It gives a lifetime 10 GiB of storage and 1 TiB of query processing a month, tables expire after 60 days, and it has no DML, streaming or Data Transfer Service. Data providers ask to join by contacting bq-public-data@google.com.
mechanisms.userFriction: A Google account and a GCP project. No card in the sandbox. Users must write SQL in the BigQuery console or a client.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 storage if accepted (Google pays). Queries are billed to the user's project.
mechanisms.costToUser: On demand: the first 1 TiB a month is free per billing account, then $6.25/TiB. Each query is billed for at least 10 MB per table referenced, so the free TiB covers roughly 100,000 minimum-size queries.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes. Query compute lands on each user's own account, and Google pays storage.
mechanisms.ops: Program application. A release job that loads each immutable release into BigQuery (or external tables over the Parquet). Google may run the copy, as it does for gnomAD.
mechanisms.limits: Acceptance is at Google's discretion. The intake path is an email, with no published criteria. The sandbox's 60-day expiry and 10 GiB cap limit joins against users' own data.

mechanisms.name: BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub) public listing: publisher pays storage, subscriber pays queries
mechanisms.what: Publish the BigQuery tables as a listing in a public data exchange. Subscribing creates a linked dataset (a pointer, not a copy) in the subscriber's own project. The docs say 'There's no additional cost for managing data exchanges or listings'. The publisher pays data storage and the subscriber pays 'Queries run against the shared data (on-demand or capacity pricing)'. Public exchanges are discoverable by all Google Cloud users and can carry free listings or commercial ones sold through Cloud Marketplace. Publishers can turn on egress restrictions that block copy, export and CREATE TABLE AS SELECT.
mechanisms.userFriction: A Google Cloud project (sandbox or billed) and a subscribe click. No genomeOS account or payment.
mechanisms.costToUs: Only BigQuery storage: active logical storage is $0.000031507/GiB-hour (about $0.023/GiB-month), and the first 10 GiB a month is free. For MB-to-GB-scale surfaces that is effectively $0.
mechanisms.costToUser: Their own query bill: 1 TiB a month free, then $6.25/TiB.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Fully, with zero billing operations. This is the cleanest way to pass query costs on for anyone who already has, or will create, a GCP project.
mechanisms.ops: A load step per release. Listing metadata. Optionally a Cloud Marketplace commercial listing later.
mechanisms.limits: Google Cloud only. Subscribers need a Google Cloud project. I did not confirm whether a sandbox project (no billing) can subscribe to a linked dataset, so test that. If the publisher uses row-level security or masking, subscribers need the Enterprise edition.

mechanisms.name: Requester Pays buckets (GCS or S3), as gnomAD does for its Hail tables and AnVIL for its data buckets
mechanisms.what: The bucket owner keeps paying storage. Each requester names a billing project and pays operations, retrieval and network egress. On GCS, 'Data storage charges ... are always applied to the project that contains the bucket', and a request without a billing project fails with 400 UserProjectMissing. On S3, anonymous access is not allowed and every request must be authenticated and carry x-amz-request-payer. gnomAD moved its Hail tables to Requester Pays in 2020 after the egress spike. AnVIL data buckets are Requester Pays too.
mechanisms.userFriction: High. Users need a cloud account, a billing account with a card, and a project with the Service Usage Consumer role, and must pass a userProject or request-payer flag. Google's free trial gives $300 for 90 days but needs a card or other payment method to verify identity.
mechanisms.costToUs: Storage only.
mechanisms.costToUser: Cloud list prices, for example GCS egress at $0.12/GiB to the internet. In-region reads from cloud compute avoid that egress.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, fully and automatically, for egress and operations.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Set one bucket flag and document the userProject parameter. scripts/fetch_data.py would need a billed client for that bucket, which loses its 'standard library only' property.
mechanisms.limits: It ends anonymous access to that bucket, so it must never be switched on for the existing free bucket. Use a separate bucket for heavy material (raw harvests, models). It excludes researchers without a cloud account.

mechanisms.name: Terra / AnVIL: users bill their own Google Cloud billing account through a Terra billing project
mechanisms.what: Every Terra billing project sits on a Google Cloud billing account that pays all workspace costs. Terra describes billing projects as 'a pass-through' at Google's standard rates and charges nothing for administration or support. Costs are tracked per workspace (each workspace has its own Google project): storage, compute, and reads from Requester Pays buckets. AnVIL data is Requester Pays and stored multi-region in the US, so in-region analysis avoids transfer charges.
mechanisms.userFriction: High. A Google billing account with a card, linked to Terra, then a billing project. Controlled-access data adds approvals on top.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 for user compute and egress. The platform operator (Broad, Verily, NHGRI) carries the platform cost.
mechanisms.costToUser: Google list prices passed through, with no markup.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, completely, via the users' own cloud accounts.
mechanisms.ops: For genomeOS, publishing a Terra-readable copy is just a Requester Pays bucket or a public bucket plus a demo workspace (gnomAD links one). Running a platform like Terra is out of scope.
mechanisms.limits: Billing data lags by hours. Removing the billing account deletes workspace data. It mostly suits users who already work in the cloud.

mechanisms.name: UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (DNAnexus on AWS): access fee plus pay-your-own compute, with credits
mechanisms.what: An analysis-in-place model. Access costs £3,000 (Tier 1), £6,000 (Tier 2) or £9,000 (Tier 3) for three years, excluding VAT, or £500 for students and researchers in lower-income countries. Users then pay compute, storage of their own uploads, and egress. Storing dispensed UKB data is free 'thanks to the generous support of Amazon Web Services'. Every researcher gets £40 of credit on joining from DNAnexus, plus an AWS-funded credits programme for early-career researchers and those in lower-income countries. Individual-level data cannot be downloaded, only summary outputs. In April 2026 UKB halted access after breaches of its Material Transfer Agreement and planned a phased reopening from September 2026, with no result downloads at first.
mechanisms.userFriction: Very high. An institutional application, an access fee, a platform account and a card or credits.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable as a model. It shows the cost split: the sponsor (AWS) pays for the hosted data, and users pay for compute.
mechanisms.costToUser: Access fee plus pay-as-you-go compute. The rate card lists a 2-vCPU spot instance at £0.0168/hour.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes: fees plus pass-through compute.
mechanisms.ops: Very high, a full trusted research environment. That is appropriate for controlled human data, not for genomeOS's open aggregates.
mechanisms.limits: The opposite of low friction. The 2026 closure shows how a single gated platform can cut every user off at once. The credit amounts differ between UKB's own pages, so check the live pages.

mechanisms.name: All of Us Researcher Workbench: starter credits, then the user's own billing account
mechanisms.what: Each newly registered researcher gets $300 in initial cloud credits. A 2026 notice says they expire 365 days after first access. When the credits run out or expire, users cannot launch environments, and stored resources may be deleted unless a Google Cloud billing account is attached. Billing is set per workspace.
mechanisms.userFriction: Starts low (no card while credits last), then becomes high (a Google billing account).
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable as a model. The sponsor (NIH) funds the starter credits.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 up to $300, then Google list prices.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Partly. A fixed exploration subsidy per user, then full pass-through.
mechanisms.ops: A credit ledger per user plus a handover to the user's own billing account.
mechanisms.limits: The handover is a cliff edge, with possible data loss if billing is not attached in time. Someone has to fund the credits.

mechanisms.name: Source Cooperative (Radiant Earth)
mechanisms.what: A 'data publishing utility' on S3-compatible storage with a public catalog and standard URLs. It says 'all data hosted in Source is available to the public and can be accessed by anyone'. In June 2025 it held over 1 PB in 300+ data products, served about 126 million requests and half a petabyte a month, and hosting was free thanks to Navigation Fund money and 'in-kind support from AWS'. A Data Proxy lets Source meter traffic, throttle access and manage authentication. The homepage still says 'Pricing plans based on data volume and usage will be announced soon'. Planned ideas include free tiers for small datasets, storage-based fees for publishers, and direct cloud access for high-bandwidth users.
mechanisms.userFriction: None for readers (public URLs, S3 tools). Publishers need a beta account or approval.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 today. Future storage fees are not yet announced.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, for now, through donors and AWS in-kind support.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Upload a mirror of each release and keep the catalog metadata.
mechanisms.limits: Beta. Pricing is unannounced. Public data only, so no paid tier.

mechanisms.name: Hugging Face Hub dataset repos (free public hosting, auto-Parquet viewer, optional gating)
mechanisms.what: Free public storage is 'best-effort' for free accounts, with 100 GB private. PRO includes up to 10 TB of public storage, Team gets 12 TB plus 1 TB per seat, and Enterprise 200 TB or more. The public storage add-on costs $12/TB-month ($10/TB at 50 TB). Storage grants exist for high-impact work. Downloads ('resolvers') are free but rate-limited per 5-minute window: 3,000 anonymous per IP, 5,000 for a free user, 12,000 for PRO. Gated datasets make a user log in and share username and email, with optional extra fields, and can approve automatically. Single files are capped at 500 GB (under 200 GB recommended), and Parquet is preferred so the dataset viewer works. Storage Buckets (an S3-like, non-versioned repo type) fall under the same storage limits.
mechanisms.userFriction: None for public files. Gated: a free HF account plus a click-through form, and a token for scripts.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 at modest size. At TB scale, PRO or Team plus the add-on, $12/TB-month.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, by putting egress on HF, so there is no need to charge.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Mirror releases as Parquet with a dataset card. Gating automation via the API.
mechanisms.limits: 'Best-effort' is not a guarantee, and HF asks that large uploads be useful to the community. Gated access is a login wall, not billing. A login-only gate may also conflict with ODP's no-gating rule if the same data is mirrored there, so gate only data that is not on ODP.

mechanisms.name: Zenodo (CERN): free archival deposits with DOIs
mechanisms.what: Free to deposit and download. Zenodo takes 'up to 50GB per record with a maximum of 100 files' and offers a one-time increase to 200 GB for a single record. Splitting one dataset across records to get around the limit is not allowed. Since April 2026, a quota increase can be requested during deposit. OpenAIRE describes funding from CERN, OpenAIRE and the European Commission, with data stored at CERN.
mechanisms.userFriction: None for downloads. Deposit needs a Zenodo account.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, via funders' infrastructure.
mechanisms.ops: Low. One deposit per citable release, with the DOI recorded in the manifest. The GitHub integration can automate it.
mechanisms.limits: 50 GB per record (200 GB once) and 100 files. HTTP download only, so it suits citation and archive, not a query backend or TB-scale harvests.

mechanisms.name: Microsoft Planetary Computer: anonymous short-lived SAS tokens, higher limits for registered users, paid 'Pro' for private data
mechanisms.what: The docs say 'The data hosted by the Planetary Computer is free for anyone to use', but some datasets need a Shared Access Signature token, and 'you don't have to be a registered Planetary Computer user to get an access token'. Registered users, and requests from the West Europe region, get better rate limits and longer token expiry. Tokens are issued per collection and are short-lived (about an hour). The STAC API is public and anonymous. The hosted Hub was retired on 6 June 2024, and the data and APIs remain. Planetary Computer Pro is a paid Azure service for private catalogs. Its pricing page lists storage, operations and bandwidth, and ingest compute as cost drivers. Pro tokens need an Entra ID bearer token.
mechanisms.userFriction: None or very low. Tokens are fetched automatically by the client library, and registration is optional for better limits.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable. Microsoft sponsors the open catalog.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 for the open catalog.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No charge for open data. The token step lets Microsoft throttle and attribute use without a login wall.
mechanisms.ops: Pattern to copy: a token-vending endpoint that issues short-lived signed URLs anonymously at a low rate, and at a higher rate to registered keys.
mechanisms.limits: Anonymous users get lower rate limits. Commercial Pro is a separate product with Entra ID auth.

mechanisms.name: OpenAlex: free bulk snapshot plus a dollar-metered API with free daily allowance, $1 prepaid top-ups and invoiced annual plans
mechanisms.what: A hybrid model and the closest template for genomeOS. (1) The full snapshot is free on S3 with no AWS account, and AWS ODP pays about $70 of transfer per download. (2) The API is 'freemium': $0.10 a day without a key and $1 a day with a free key (create an account and copy the key, no payment method needed). The budget resets at midnight UTC. Single-record lookups are free, list calls cost $0.0001 and search $0.001. (3) Prepaid usage is self-serve 'in $1 increments, by card', is used only after the free daily budget, and 'expires 3 months after your most recent purchase'. A VAT invoice is available. (4) Annual plans (Member at $5,000 a year with a $20/day budget, plus Member+ and Partner) are sold by quote, purchase order and invoice for institutions. (5) Daily-refreshed snapshots are a paid enterprise feature. When the budget runs out, requests return a rate-limit error until the reset.
mechanisms.userFriction: Tiered. Anonymous for the snapshot and light API use. Email sign-up for 10x the allowance. A card only once beyond $1 a day. Purchase order and invoice for institutions.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable as a model. AWS ODP absorbs bulk egress, so the API is the only metered cost.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 for most users. Pay as you go above $1 a day.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes. Heavy API users fund API compute, and bulk users cost the publisher nothing because of ODP.
mechanisms.ops: Medium. Key issuance, a per-key dollar ledger, a cost per call type, card checkout and sales-led invoicing.
mechanisms.limits: Earlier credit-unit pricing was replaced by dollars, so third-party pages quoting credits are out of date. Prepaid balances expire.

mechanisms.name: Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem: free quotas with login, throttled rather than cut off, commercial top-up via CREODIAS
mechanisms.what: Every registered Copernicus General user gets 12 TB of transfer per rolling 30 days at 20 MB/s per connection with 4 connections. Over the limit, bandwidth drops to 1 MB/s and 1 connection, so downloads still work, just slower. Users also get 10,000 Sentinel Hub requests and 10,000 processing units a month, 50,000 direct COG requests a month, and 10,000 openEO credits on the first of each month. More capacity comes from commercial cloud credits, sponsorship applications, or subscriptions bought through CREODIAS.
mechanisms.userFriction: A free account. No card for the free quota.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable. Funded by the EU and ESA.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 within quota. Paid CREODIAS subscriptions above it.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Partly. Heavy users buy commercial capacity from an operator partner.
mechanisms.ops: A pattern to copy: quotas per account, with a throttle instead of a hard error.
mechanisms.limits: Needs an account even for light use. Extended-quota prices are not published.

mechanisms.name: Google Earth Engine noncommercial tiers (since 27 April 2026)
mechanisms.what: Monthly compute quotas per project, reset on the first of the month. Community: 150 EECU-hours, for any verified noncommercial project. Contributor: 1,000 EECU-hours if the project has an active billing account, and 'Noncommercial Earth Engine usage isn't charged to that account'. Partner: 100,000 EECU-hours by application, for climate work. The quotas 'are not hard cut-off values'. Once a project uses its quota it enters a restricted mode with less concurrency until the reset. More capacity means switching to a commercial pay-as-you-go 'Limited' plan.
mechanisms.userFriction: A Google account and a verified noncommercial project. Attaching a card (not charged) raises the quota about 7x.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable. Google sponsors it.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 for noncommercial use. Paid only if the project goes commercial.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Through commercial users. Noncommercial use is subsidised.
mechanisms.ops: A pattern to copy: 'add a payment method to unlock more free quota' screens out abuse without charging anyone.
mechanisms.limits: Throttling slows heavy users rather than billing them.

mechanisms.name: GBIF: free downloads behind a free login, each download minted a DOI
mechanisms.what: Data 'is free for all—but not free of obligations'. Occurrence downloads need a GBIF.org account. Each download made through the website or rgbif occ_download() gets a DOI, and the account keeps a download history. Search-API pulls get no DOI. Users can register a 'derived dataset' DOI after logging in.
mechanisms.userFriction: A free account. No card.
mechanisms.costToUs: Not applicable. Funded by its participant countries.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No, but the login and DOI give attribution and usage evidence that help with funding renewals.
mechanisms.ops: Asynchronous download jobs, plus DOI minting per extract (for example through DataCite or Zenodo).
mechanisms.limits: A login wall for bulk extracts.

mechanisms.name: Cloudflare R2 zero-egress mirror
mechanisms.what: S3-compatible object storage. Standard storage costs $0.015/GB-month, Class A operations $4.50 per million and Class B $0.36 per million, and egress is free, including through r2.dev. The free tier gives 10 GB-month, 1 million Class A and 10 million Class B operations a month. The r2.dev subdomain 'is rate-limited and should only be used for development purposes'. Production traffic should use a custom domain, which also enables Cloudflare cache, WAF and access controls (Zero Trust Access, WAF Token Authentication).
mechanisms.userFriction: None (public HTTPS).
mechanisms.costToUs: About $0 at the current data size. Storage is $0.015/GB-month, egress is $0, and reads are $0.36 per million after the free 10 million.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: It removes egress cost rather than recovering it. A mirror the Atlas site and fetch_data.py could read first, keeping GCS as the source of truth.
mechanisms.ops: Low to medium. A sync job after each release, a custom domain (needs Cloudflare DNS), and keeping sha256 verification against the manifest.
mechanisms.limits: A second vendor. Pulling from GCS to R2 once per release still pays GCS egress for that copy. Gating on R2 needs Cloudflare Access or WAF configuration.

mechanisms.name: Stripe prepaid credits (Checkout top-ups into our own ledger, or Stripe billing credits with Meters)
mechanisms.what: Two ways to build it. (a) The simplest: one-time Stripe Checkout payments buy credits held in our own per-account ledger, which is debited for metered queries and downloads. (b) Stripe-native: Credit Grants ('Grant billing credits ... that they can use to pay for usage-based products') applied to a $0 subscription with a metered price and usage reported through Meters. Credit grants only apply to subscription items with metered prices that report through Meters, not to one-off invoices. Credits can carry an expires_at date, and there is a limit of 100 unused grants per customer. Stripe forbids using billing credits as stored value, gift cards or for third-party purchases. Stripe now also offers Metronome for complex usage billing.
mechanisms.userFriction: Medium. A card entered once, through Stripe Checkout, Apple Pay or Google Pay, only when a user goes past the free allowance.
mechanisms.costToUs: Cards: 2.9% + 30¢ per successful domestic charge, +1.5% for international cards, +1% if currency conversion is needed, +0.5% if the card is typed in manually. ACH: 0.8%, capped at $5. Stripe Billing pay-as-you-go: 0.7% of billing volume (option b only, and one-off invoices are excluded). Stripe Tax: 0.5% per transaction where registered. Worked example: a $10 domestic top-up costs $0.59 (5.9%), or $0.74 on an international card. A $25 top-up costs $1.03 (4.1%). So set a $10-$25 minimum rather than metering cents.
mechanisms.costToUser: Cost plus the payment fee, rounded up to whole credits.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, before the cost is incurred: no bad debt and no dunning. That is safer than postpaid metering for a project with a $200 budget.
mechanisms.ops: Medium. Webhooks, a ledger with idempotent debits, refunds, receipts and VAT invoices, and sales tax or VAT registration where required. Keep usage pricing in a reviewed table, as OpenAlex prices per call type.
mechanisms.limits: The fixed 30¢ fee makes small top-ups expensive. Selling digital services across borders may create VAT or GST obligations, which a merchant of record can absorb (see below). This is not legal or tax advice.

mechanisms.name: Merchant of record (Paddle, or Stripe Managed Payments) to offload international tax
mechanisms.what: The merchant of record is the legal seller. It collects and remits sales tax, VAT and GST, and handles fraud, disputes and buyer support. Paddle charges '5% + 50¢ per Checkout transaction' with no monthly fees. Stripe Managed Payments 'adds 3.5% per successful transaction to your standard Stripe processing fees', covering tax in 80+ countries, fraud prevention and dispute responses.
mechanisms.userFriction: The same as card checkout.
mechanisms.costToUs: Paddle: a $10 top-up costs $1.00 (10%) and a $25 top-up $1.75 (7%). Stripe Managed Payments: a $10 top-up costs about $0.94 (Stripe's $0.59 plus 3.5%).
mechanisms.costToUser: Fee passed through in the credit price.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, and it removes most of the tax-compliance overhead of selling to researchers worldwide.
mechanisms.ops: Lower than running our own tax compliance. Higher fee per transaction.
mechanisms.limits: Higher percentage fees. Makes small top-ups even less efficient.

mechanisms.name: Institutional plans by quote, purchase order and invoice
mechanisms.what: Institutions often cannot use cards, and buy by quote, PO and invoice. OpenAlex sells annual plans this way ('Institutions often need quotes, purchase orders, and invoices'). Its Member plan costs $5,000 a year with a $20/day API budget. Stripe Invoicing costs 0.4% per paid invoice (Starter) or 0.5% (Plus), with no fixed fees, plus payment-method fees (ACH 0.8% capped at $5) and auto-reconciliation of ACH credit and wire payments. Hugging Face Academia Hub is a subscription bought by university IT, priced 'based on volume of usage and number of active users'. A Hub docs pull request lists $10 per seat per month, which I have not verified. CILogon's paid tiers ($16,547 and $38,610 a year in 2026) show what institutional subscriptions for research infrastructure cost.
mechanisms.userFriction: None for the individual researcher once the institution has bought. Weeks of procurement for the buyer.
mechanisms.costToUs: Stripe Invoicing 0.4% plus ACH 0.8% (capped at $5), or wire fees. Mostly staff time on quotes.
mechanisms.costToUser: An annual fee paid by the lab or library, not the individual.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, and it can fund the free tier for everyone else, as institutional memberships do at OpenAlex and ORCID.
mechanisms.ops: Medium. Quotes, PO handling, renewals and a membership roster tied to logins (for example by email domain or institutional IdP through CILogon).
mechanisms.limits: A slow sales cycle. Only worth it once usage justifies it.

mechanisms.name: ORCID sign-in (Public API vs Member API)
mechanisms.what: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect sign-in that returns an authenticated ORCID iD, the researcher identifier most likely to be accepted. The Public API is free and gives 100,000 reads a day per client and 12 requests a second, with HTTPS redirect URIs only. But it is 'free for non-commercial use by individuals', and the terms say 'you may not make use of the public APIs in connection with any revenue-generating product or service'. ORCID also 'reserves the right to ... require membership and associated fees for extensive or extended use'. The Member API needs a paid organisational membership, with a 20% discount for non-profits and government and 75% for organisations under $200,000 revenue. A secondary source puts 2026 Basic non-profit membership at about $4,775 a year, which I have not verified.
mechanisms.userFriction: Very low for researchers: one click with an account most already have.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 on the Public API for the free tier. Membership fees if sign-in is used for the paid, cost-recovery tier, which is how the terms read. Ask ORCID before relying on it.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Not applicable (identity only).
mechanisms.ops: Register a client per individual developer record (credentials cannot be transferred), handle redirect URIs, and map iDs to accounts.
mechanisms.limits: The licence terms conflict with paid use. ORCID iDs carry no billing or institutional affiliation by default. If ORCID is set up as a generic OIDC provider in Google Identity Platform, it costs $0.015 per MAU after 50.

mechanisms.name: Federated research login: CILogon, or Google Identity Platform with Google and GitHub social login
mechanisms.what: CILogon's Basic tier is an OpenID Connect provider with 'No charge for academic research projects' (manual client registration, best-effort support). It federates InCommon and eduGAIN, and user guides list Google, GitHub, ORCID and Microsoft as login choices. Paid tiers cost $16,547 and $38,610 a year. Google Identity Platform (which fits the existing GCP project) charges nothing for the first 50,000 MAU on email and social providers such as Google and GitHub, then $0.0055 per MAU. Generic OIDC and SAML providers (ORCID, institutional SSO) are free for 50 MAU, then $0.015 per MAU.
mechanisms.userFriction: Very low. One click with an existing Google, GitHub, institutional or ORCID account. No new password.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 at expected scale (social login under 50,000 MAU, or CILogon Basic).
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Not applicable. This is the identity layer under keys and credits.
mechanisms.ops: Low. One OIDC integration, plus account and API-key issuance.
mechanisms.limits: A security write-up of the JupyterHub CILogon authenticator found it checked only the email address, not which provider issued it. So never authorise institutional plans on email domain alone. Check the IdP or the affiliation claim. CILogon Basic is best-effort support.

mechanisms.name: Signed URLs to gate paid or heavy downloads from a private bucket
mechanisms.what: A small authorising service checks a user's key or credit balance, debits the ledger by object size, and returns a short-lived GCS V4 signed URL. 'The longest expiration value is 604800 seconds (7 days).' The bytes go straight from GCS to the user. The service never proxies data, so it stays tiny and needs no inference on the serving path.
mechanisms.userFriction: An API key or session. No cloud account.
mechanisms.costToUs: GCS egress at $0.12/GiB (recovered from the user's credits) plus a negligible signing service.
mechanisms.costToUser: Egress at cost plus the payment fee, drawn from prepaid credits.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, for bulk downloads by users who have no cloud account.
mechanisms.ops: Medium. A signing service account with a narrow scope, ledger debits that are idempotent, and pricing by object size from the release manifest (bytes are already recorded).
mechanisms.limits: Partial or ranged reads of signed URLs make byte-exact metering hard, so charge per object. Leaked URLs keep working until they expire, so keep expiries short.

mechanisms.name: Client-side SQL over the free Parquet (DuckDB, including DuckDB-WASM in the browser)
mechanisms.what: DuckDB 'supports partial reading ... a combination of the Parquet metadata and HTTP range requests', and fetches only what a query needs. 'SELECT column_a' reads only the metadata and that column, and a count(*) reads no data at all. Exploring the free tier through DuckDB (CLI, Python or WASM in the Atlas site) therefore needs no server-side query engine and moves only a small share of the bytes.
mechanisms.userFriction: None. A URL, or the Atlas site.
mechanisms.costToUs: Egress on the bytes actually read, a small share of the full download. $0 compute.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0. Runs on the user's own machine.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: It keeps costs near zero rather than recovering them. It is the main reason exploration can stay free and anonymous.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Lay out Parquet for pruning (row groups sorted by variant and H3 cell, sensible row-group sizes) and publish a schema and example queries.
mechanisms.limits: Not suited to multi-TB scans or joins. Those should go to BYO-cloud BigQuery or Requester Pays.

mechanisms.name: Cloud research credits that make 'bring your own cloud' affordable for users
mechanisms.what: Google Cloud research credits give faculty and postdocs one award of up to $5,000, and PhD students up to $1,000 once a year. They expire 365 days after redemption, cannot be used commercially, and are open to accredited institutions in approved countries. Google's free trial gives $300 for 90 days but needs a card or other payment method to verify identity. UKB-RAP and All of Us show how sponsor-funded starter credits work.
mechanisms.userFriction: A short proposal (research credits) or a card for identity checks (trial).
mechanisms.costToUs: $0. Google funds them.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 up to the credit amount.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Indirectly. They pay users' own Analytics Hub queries or Requester Pays egress.
mechanisms.ops: None. Link to them from the access page.
mechanisms.limits: Eligibility is restricted. Credits run out after a year.

research: peer providers.notes:
RECOMMENDED SHAPE: draw the free/paid line by cost driver, not by dataset. Comparable providers keep data free and charge, or move costs onto users, only for heavy compute or bulk volume.

TIER 0, anonymous and free for good. Every released file (registries, observation counts, surfaces cells.parquet, validation evidence, manifests) stays on the public genomeos-atlas-data and genomeos-atlas-web buckets. scripts/fetch_data.py stays unchanged. This meets the owner's 'current datasets fine to distribute this way'.
- Add free mirrors so heavy downloaders cost us nothing and the data survives a kill-switch trip:
  - AWS ODP pays S3 storage and egress (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
  - Hugging Face public Parquet repo, free best-effort public storage (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-limits).
  - Source Cooperative, free while its pricing is 'announced soon' (https://source.coop/).
  - Zenodo for DOIs, up to 50 GB per record (https://support.zenodo.org/help/en-gb/1-upload-deposit/80-what-are-the-size-limitations-of-zenodo).
  - Optionally a Cloudflare R2 mirror with $0 egress (https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/).
- Releases are MB-scale today. At GCS $0.12/GiB (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing), the $200 budget covers about 1.6 TiB of egress a month.
- Point exploration at client-side DuckDB over HTTP range requests, which reads only the needed columns (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/httpfs/https.html).

TIER 1, free with one-click sign-in, for the hosted query layer.
- Use Google or GitHub social login through Identity Platform ($0 under 50,000 MAU) or CILogon Basic ('No charge for academic research projects').
- Give a daily allowance metered in dollars, as OpenAlex does: $0.10 a day without a key, $1 a day with a free key (https://help.openalex.org/api-reference/authentication).
- When the allowance runs out, throttle rather than refuse:
  - Copernicus drops to 1 MB/s after 12 TB in 30 days (https://documentation.dataspace.copernicus.eu/Quotas.html).
  - Earth Engine quotas 'are not hard cut-off values' (https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/noncommercial_tiers).
- What a key buys us: abuse control, attribution and usage evidence for funders, with no card.

TIER 2, bring your own cloud: zero cost and zero billing work for us.
- A BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub) public listing. We pay only storage and subscribers pay their own queries: 1 TiB a month free, then $6.25/TiB (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-introduction, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).
- Apply to the Google Cloud Public Datasets Program so that Google pays storage (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data).
- A separate Requester Pays bucket for raw harvests and trained models (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).
- Never turn on Requester Pays for the existing free bucket: it ends anonymous access.

TIER 3, prepaid credits for people without a cloud account.
- Stripe Checkout one-time top-ups into our own ledger, with a $10-$25 minimum. Card fees are 2.9% + 30¢, +1.5% for international cards (https://stripe.com/pricing). A $10 top-up loses $0.59.
- Spend credits on metered queries and on signed-URL bulk downloads priced at egress cost (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls).
- Prepay rather than invoice in arrears, so there is no bad debt.
- Expire balances on a long horizon. OpenAlex sells $1 increments that expire 3 months after the last purchase (https://help.openalex.org/access/buying-and-renewing/).
- Consider a merchant of record (Paddle 5% + 50¢, https://www.paddle.com/pricing; Stripe Managed Payments +3.5%, https://stripe.com/managed-payments) to avoid registering for VAT and GST abroad.

TIER 4, institutions.
- Annual plans by quote, PO and invoice. OpenAlex Member is $5,000 a year with a $20/day budget (https://help.openalex.org/access/buying-and-renewing/). Stripe Invoicing costs 0.4% per paid invoice (https://stripe.com/invoicing/pricing).
- Waive fees or grant credits for students and lower-income countries. UKB-RAP and All of Us are the precedents.

FRICTION LADDER, from least to most, as seen across providers:
1. Anonymous URL.
2. Short-lived anonymous token (Planetary Computer, https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/docs/concepts/sas).
3. One-click OAuth plus API key.
4. Click-through terms (HF gated datasets, GBIF).
5. A card entered once.
6. A cloud billing account. Google needs a card even for the $300 trial (https://cloud.google.com/signup-faqs?hl=en).
7. An institutional application plus a platform (UKB-RAP).

Each step loses users. So the card and cloud-account steps should only appear once someone exceeds a generous free allowance, never on first contact.

LICENCE INTERACTIONS THAT CONSTRAIN THE LINE:
- AWS ODP refuses non-commercial licences and gated access (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/). So fields flagged in genomeos/publication/commercial_use.py (gnomad.spliceai, alphagenome.top_attributions) and any 'restricted' source cannot go on an ODP mirror.
- Charging even cost-recovery fees for CC BY-NC material is ambiguous. CC defines NC as 'not primarily intended for ... monetary compensation' (https://wiki.creativecommons.org/NonCommercial_interpretation). Some guides accept cost recovery (https://opentextbc.ca/faqs/?p=188), but confirm with the licensor.
- Safest: charge for compute and transfer as a service, keep non_commercial fields free-only or out of paid products, and drive this from the existing per-release terms register.
- ORCID's free Public API may not be used 'in connection with any revenue-generating product or service' (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/). Use ORCID login for the free tier only, ask ORCID about cost recovery, or budget for membership.

UNVERIFIED OR CONFLICTING, check before relying on them:
- Whether a BigQuery sandbox project (no billing) can subscribe to an Analytics Hub listing.
- ORCID's 2026 membership price (secondary source only).
- Hugging Face Academia Hub at $10 per seat (from a docs pull request).
- UKB credit amounts (UKB's pages disagree).
- Source Cooperative's future pricing.
- Whether Google bills for responses served from its edge caches (already open in docs/cost-controls.md).

No cloud commands were run and no files were written. The repository context came from docs/data-store.md, docs/cost-controls.md, scripts/build_data_release.py and genomeos/publication/commercial_use.py on origin/main.

mechanisms.name: Anonymous public GCS bucket (what runs today), with an optional billing project
mechanisms.what: Keep the current public-read data-store bucket (genomeos-atlas-data) as the free tier: plain HTTPS GETs on https://storage.googleapis.com/<bucket>/<key>, hash-pinned by the committed manifests, with no login. GCS also lets any caller who sends a billing project pay for their own request on a bucket that does NOT have Requester Pays turned on: 'Buckets that have Requester Pays disabled still accept requests that include a billing project, and charges are applied to the billing project supplied in the request.' So heavy users and CI jobs can choose to pay for their own egress from the same free bucket, without a second bucket.
mechanisms.userFriction: None for the default path: Python standard library, no account, no key. The optional pay-my-own-way path needs a Google login and a project with billing enabled (same as Requester Pays below).
mechanisms.costToUs: Internet egress from the bucket is $0.12/GiB for the first 10 TiB per month to worldwide destinations other than Asia and Australia ($0.19/GiB to Australia, $0.23/GiB to China). Standard storage in us-east1 is $0.000027397/GiB-hour, about $0.02/GiB-month. Class B (read) operations are $0.0004 per 1,000 in a single region. Always Free covers 5 GB-months of storage, 50,000 Class B operations and '100 GB from North America to each Google Cloud Data transfer destination (Australia and China excluded)' each month, in us-east1, us-central1 and us-west1. At about 0.27 GB per release, a full download costs about $0.03, so after the 100 GB free allowance the $200 budget covers roughly 1,600 GiB, or about 6,000 full downloads a month.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No, except where a user chooses to send a billing project. The bucket owner pays egress and operations for every anonymous read.
mechanisms.ops: Already running: budget, kill switch (docs/cost-controls.md), and the stdlib fetch_data.py. To support the optional path, fetch_data.py would gain a --billing-project flag that sends the same headers as Requester Pays below.
mechanisms.limits: There is no per-user metering or rate limit, so one heavy downloader can trip the kill switch for everyone. Billing data lags by hours. Egress is billed on the bytes actually served, so ranged Parquet reads cost less than whole-file GETs.

mechanisms.name: GCS Requester Pays bucket (the paid tier, billed by Google)
mechanisms.what: A second bucket with Requester Pays turned on holds the expensive objects: raw third-party harvests, trained models, and large derived products. The requester's project pays the 'Data processing charges for operations, replication, and data retrieval' and 'Network usage charges for reading the data'. The bucket owner always pays storage: 'Data storage charges, including early deletion charges, are always applied to the project that contains the bucket.' Only two kinds of request are accepted: (1) requests that include a billing project, made by a user who holds serviceusage.services.use (the Service Usage Consumer role) on that project, and (2) owner-side callers with createBillingAssignment. 'All other requests to the bucket fail with a 400 UserProjectMissing error.' Anonymous reads therefore always fail, so the free/paid line has to be a bucket boundary. How the billing project is passed: in the XML API, a GET on https://storage.googleapis.com/BUCKET/OBJECT with the headers 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' and 'x-goog-user-project: <PROJECT>'. In the JSON API, https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/b/BUCKET/o/<url-encoded OBJECT>?alt=media&userProject=<PROJECT>. A stdlib-only client (fetch_data.py) needs an OAuth access token, and has three ways to get one without new dependencies: (a) read it from an env var that the user fills with `gcloud auth print-access-token`; (b) read the authorized_user ADC file at ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json and POST its refresh_token to https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token with urllib; (c) on a GCE VM or Cloud Run, ask the metadata server. A service-account JSON key needs an RS256 JWT, which the Python stdlib cannot sign, so that path needs google-auth or gcloud. DuckDB's httpfs can send the same headers through CREATE SECRET (TYPE http, EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS MAP{...}), so SQL over Parquet ranges should also work (not tested). Precedent: gnomAD in 2020 moved its Hail tables to a requester-pays bucket and kept VCFs and small files free.
mechanisms.userFriction: Medium-high. The user needs a Google account, a GCP project with billing enabled (a payment card; new accounts get $300 of trial credit for 90 days, and academics can apply for $5,000 research credits), the Service Usage Consumer role on that project, and either gcloud or an access token. Some institution-managed Google accounts cannot create projects without their organization.
mechanisms.costToUs: Storage only (about $0.02/GiB-month Standard in us-east1). Requests are free to us.
mechanisms.costToUser: Exactly Google's list price, with no markup: $0.12/GiB to the internet (about $0.03 per 0.27 GB release), $0 data transfer when reading from compute in the same region (US-EAST1 to US-EAST1 is free), $0.02/GiB to other North American regions, and $0.0004 per 1,000 Class B reads.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, and fully for egress and operations, because Google bills the requester's own billing account directly. We never touch money, set prices or invoice. Storage stays with us.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Create one bucket, turn on Requester Pays, and grant read to allAuthenticatedUsers (or allUsers; anonymous reads fail either way). Add --billing-project plus token handling to fetch_data.py, and record each object's tier and bucket in the manifest. This bucket needs no kill switch, since egress isn't ours.
mechanisms.limits: Cannot be used for Cloud SQL import/export or Pub/Sub export. Requesters' bills don't itemize these charges separately; Google suggests a dedicated project. We can't give credits or discounts, and we can't meter per user beyond the audit logs. Signed URLs against a Requester Pays bucket presumably need userProject in the signed request; that is not verified. The friction is out of proportion for tiny files, so keep anything under about 1 GB in the free tier.

mechanisms.name: BigQuery dataset shared with allAuthenticatedUsers (querier pays, usually $0)
mechanisms.what: Load the observation, surface and registry Parquet into native BigQuery tables in our project and give dataset read to the special group allAuthenticatedUsers, which dataset access policies support. Anyone signed in to Google can then query genomeos-project.dataset.table from their own project. BigQuery bills the job's project: 'You are charged for queries run against shared data. The data owner is not charged when their data is accessed.' Every billing account gets the first 1 TiB of query processing free each month. The BigQuery sandbox lets a user do this 'without providing a credit card or creating a billing account'. This is the lowest-friction SQL tier that still costs us almost nothing.
mechanisms.userFriction: Low. A Google account, plus a one-time sandbox project created in the console (no card). After that it's console SQL, the bq CLI, or client libraries. Institution-managed accounts must pick an organization when they create the project.
mechanisms.costToUs: Storage only: the first 10 GiB per month is free, then active logical storage is $0.000031507/GiB-hour (about $0.023/GiB-month). Our tables are well under 10 GiB. Use native tables, not external tables over the us-east1 bucket: GCS treats BigQuery US as us-central1, so 'data transfer out charges will apply when BigQuery US reads data from any other Cloud Storage bucket', and those reads would land on our bill every time anyone queries. Either load the data once, or put the dataset in the bucket's region.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 within 1 TiB processed per month per billing account. After that, on-demand queries cost $6.25/TiB. Each query is billed at least 10 MB per table referenced. The sandbox has a lifetime limit of 10 GiB of the user's own storage, and their tables expire after 60 days.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes. Query compute is always billed to the querier, and Google's free tier absorbs almost all of it. Storage stays with us and is free at our size.
mechanisms.ops: Low. A publish step loads each immutable release into versioned tables (or one dataset per release), applies partitioning and clustering (for example by variant or H3 parent) so scans stay small, and sets the dataset's access entry. No serving infrastructure.
mechanisms.limits: Users need a Google account, so it isn't anonymous. Not tested: whether a sandbox project can query a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset (expected yes). BigQuery's SQL dialect differs from DuckDB's. Downloading results in bulk through the Storage Read API can still incur egress.

mechanisms.name: BigQuery sharing (formerly Analytics Hub): free public listing
mechanisms.what: Publish the BigQuery dataset as a listing in a public data exchange, shared with allAuthenticatedUsers, so it appears in Google's data catalog. Subscribers create a read-only 'linked dataset' in their own project without copying any data. 'There's no additional cost for managing data exchanges or listings.' The publisher pays storage, and subscribers pay for the queries they run. Publishers can see usage metrics: jobs, bytes processed, and consumption by subscriber project and organization.
mechanisms.userFriction: Low to medium. Same as the plain shared dataset, plus a one-click 'Subscribe' that creates a linked dataset in the user's project.
mechanisms.costToUs: Storage only. Listings are free.
mechanisms.costToUser: Their own query costs, inside the 1 TiB/month free tier.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, the same way as the shared dataset: queriers pay compute.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Turn on the Analytics Hub API, create an exchange and listing, and keep the listing description and documentation current.
mechanisms.limits: 'A shared dataset can have a maximum of 1,000 linked datasets', which caps adoption, so keep the direct allAuthenticatedUsers dataset as well. Linked datasets don't support materialized views or snapshots. Joins over linked datasets larger than 1 TB of physical storage may fail. Row-level security or data masking would force subscribers onto Enterprise editions.

mechanisms.name: Commercial BigQuery sharing listing sold as a Google Cloud Marketplace data product
mechanisms.what: Turn a BigQuery sharing listing into a Marketplace data product through the Producer Portal. Google handles the transaction and bills subscribers on their Google Cloud bill. Access to the linked dataset is gated by an active Marketplace order. The documented pricing models are free, subscription (a flat fee, prorated for partial months), and private offers or custom quotes; usage-based pricing for data products is not documented. Google's fee is the Marketplace revenue share: for a Standard Offer the vendor's net revenue is 97% (a 3% fee). Private offers drop to 2% for $1M-$10M deals and 1.5% for $10M+ deals, and renewals and migrations are 1.5%. That schedule took effect April 21, 2025, and Google pays the vendor the net amount.
mechanisms.userFriction: High for academics: a billing account, the Billing Account Administrator role to subscribe to a paid listing, and a Marketplace purchase flow. Any project on the same billing account can then subscribe.
mechanisms.costToUs: 3% of revenue, plus storage, plus the effort of onboarding as a vendor.
mechanisms.costToUser: The subscription price, plus their own query costs.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Only as a flat subscription, not metered per query or download. It isn't a good fit for 'just enough to recoup'.
mechanisms.ops: Heavy. The organization 'must join and maintain good standing in Google Cloud Partner Network', be incorporated in a supported region, and hold a Marketplace vendor account and payment profile. The product must be 'production-ready' and 'enterprise-ready (professional online presence, a defined sales motion, customer support)', must pass a business-case review (otherwise Google 'might offer you an adjusted revenue share'), and must attest that it contains no 'personally identifiable sensitive information' under PADFA 2024. That Act's definition of sensitive data lists 'Genetic information'. Aggregate per-population allele counts aren't linkable to individuals, but the attestation still has to be made. Publisher and subscriber must both be in Marketplace agency jurisdictions.
mechanisms.limits: Clean rooms and Pub/Sub aren't supported. Billing metrics aren't in the provider usage metrics or INFORMATION_SCHEMA. All BigQuery sharing limits apply, including 1,000 linked datasets per shared dataset.

mechanisms.name: Login + Cloud Run signed-URL broker + our own metering and payment (Stripe)
mechanisms.what: A small Cloud Run service checks the user's ID token (see Identity below), checks their entitlement or prepaid balance, logs bytes per user, and returns a V4 signed URL for the object, which can last up to 604,800 seconds (7 days). The service signs without a stored key by calling the IAM signBlob method as its own service account. Data then flows directly from GCS to the user. The payment side is done by us: Stripe card charges of 2.9% + 30¢ per successful domestic transaction (+1.5% for international cards) and, for usage-based billing, Stripe Billing at 0.7% of billing volume on pay-as-you-go. This is the only mechanism here that lets a user with no GCP account pay per GB.
mechanisms.userFriction: Medium. Sign in with Google or GitHub, enter a card once (or buy prepaid credits), then use the URLs with any HTTP client, including the stdlib fetch_data.py. No GCP account needed.
mechanisms.costToUs: Cloud Run is usually free at this scale: with request-based billing, the first 2M requests, 180,000 vCPU-seconds and 360,000 GiB-seconds each month are free. Egress through signed URLs is ours, at $0.12/GiB. Payment fees: a $10 prepaid top-up costs about $0.59 in card fees plus about $0.07 in Billing fees (about 6.6%). Charging per download (about $0.03) is impossible because the 30¢ fixed fee is ten times the cost being recovered.
mechanisms.costToUser: Our cost plus a markup that covers payment fees, best sold as prepaid credits or a monthly invoice with a minimum.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Yes, but only through our own metering, pricing and payment collection.
mechanisms.ops: Highest. We'd build and run auth, a usage ledger, pricing, Stripe integration, receipts, refunds, sales tax/VAT, a merchant entity, support and abuse handling. Signed URLs keep working after the kill switch removes allUsers, because they authorize as the signing service account (inferred), so the broker needs its own monthly spend cap.
mechanisms.limits: Anyone holding a signed URL can use it until it expires. Charging fees we collect for sources flagged non_commercial, or for ORCID-authenticated users (see Identity), may breach those terms.

mechanisms.name: Identity: Identity Platform / Firebase Authentication (Google, GitHub, ORCID by OIDC)
mechanisms.what: Managed sign-in for the broker or website. Google and GitHub are built-in providers and count as 'Social', which is Tier 1. ORCID would be a generic OpenID Connect provider, which is Tier 2. ORCID's discovery document gives issuer https://orcid.org, scopes ['openid'], code and implicit flows, token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported ['client_secret_post'] only, and claims that include name and sub but no email. Users would therefore be keyed on their ORCID iD, and accounts can't be linked by email.
mechanisms.userFriction: Very low: one click with an existing Google or GitHub account.
mechanisms.costToUs: With Identity Platform, Tier 1 (email, phone, anonymous, social) is free for the first 50,000 MAU, then $0.0055/MAU up to 100,000. Tier 2 (OIDC/SAML) is free for 50 MAU per project, then $0.015/MAU; 1,000 ORCID users a month would cost about $14. SMS is billed per message. On Firebase's no-cost Spark plan the daily limits are 3,000 Tier 1 DAU and 2 Tier 2 DAU, so ORCID needs the billing-enabled Blaze plan or Identity Platform.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No. Identity only, no billing.
mechanisms.ops: Low. Configure the providers (a GitHub OAuth app, an ORCID public API client), and have Cloud Run verify ID tokens.
mechanisms.limits: ORCID's Public API terms say the APIs are 'a free service' for non-commercial use, and 'you may not make use of the public APIs in connection with any revenue-generating product or service'. ORCID 'may require membership and associated fees for extensive or extended use'. That means ORCID sign-in is safe for the free tiers but needs ORCID's confirmation (or membership) before it gates a paid tier. Not tested: whether Identity Platform's OIDC code flow works with ORCID's client_secret_post-only token endpoint.

mechanisms.name: Cloud CDN in front of the free bucket
mechanisms.what: A global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN and the bucket as its backend. This cuts the cost of free-tier egress; it doesn't recover anything. Cloud Storage data transfer charges are waived for Cloud CDN, but cache fill applies. It would also enable the custom domain (data.genome-os.org) that the data-store design deferred.
mechanisms.userFriction: None (anonymous).
mechanisms.costToUs: Cache egress to North America is $0.08/GiB for the first 10 TiB, then $0.055/GiB. Cache fill is $0.01/GiB within North America or Europe. Cache lookups are $0.0075 per 10,000. Forwarding rules are $0.025/hour for the first 5 (about $18/month). Load balancer outbound data processing is $0.008/GiB for traffic that misses the cache. By our arithmetic, CDN only pays for itself above roughly 500 GiB/month of egress.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No. It lowers our cost by about a third per GiB at volume.
mechanisms.ops: Medium: a load balancer, a managed certificate, DNS, and cache headers (cache-control is already set to public, max-age=3600). The kill switch would also need to cover the CDN path.
mechanisms.limits: A fixed monthly cost regardless of traffic, which isn't worth it at today's volume.

mechanisms.name: API Gateway / Cloud Endpoints (metering and quotas only)
mechanisms.what: A managed proxy in front of a Cloud Run query API, with OpenAPI-defined quotas such as requests per minute. Each call is reported to Service Control.
mechanisms.userFriction: High if quotas are used: 'Each application that calls your API must: Have a Google Cloud project. Have enabled your API in their Google Cloud project. Send an API key', and 'you must have one project for each API consumer.'
mechanisms.costToUs: API Gateway and Endpoints: $0 for the first 2M calls per month per billing account, then $3.00 per million up to 1B calls, then $1.50 per million.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: No. Calls are counted and throttled (over-limit calls get 429s), but nobody is billed.
mechanisms.ops: Low to medium: an OpenAPI config, a gateway deployment, and API keys.
mechanisms.limits: Quotas are per consumer project and per minute only. API Gateway's request size limit is 32 MB, so file downloads should be redirects to signed URLs or the buckets. Per-user metering is easier to do inside the Cloud Run broker.

mechanisms.name: Apigee API monetization
mechanisms.what: A full API-management product with rate plans, prepaid or postpaid developer wallets, developer portals and AppGroups.
mechanisms.userFriction: Medium: a developer-portal sign-up, an API key, and a wallet top-up.
mechanisms.costToUs: Pay-as-you-go environments cost $365/month per region (Base, 50 QPS, Standard proxies only), $1,460 (Intermediate) or $3,431 (Comprehensive). API calls cost $20 per 1M on Standard proxies or $100 per 1M on Extensible proxies, and API Analytics is $20 per 1M calls. Monetization itself is a Subscription-only add-on: 'Apigee monetization is not available with Pay-as-you-go organizations', and the subscription price is only available from sales. The base environment alone is more than our $200/month budget.
mechanisms.costToUser: Whatever rate plan we set.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Only partly. Apigee meters usage and debits prepaid wallets, but 'Apigee does not provide any specific invoice generation functionality for billing. You handle the billing settlement with your developers.' We'd still need a payment processor.
mechanisms.ops: Heavy.
mechanisms.limits: Out of proportion to a research data project. Not recommended.

mechanisms.name: Google Cloud Public Datasets Program
mechanisms.what: Google hosts accepted open datasets in its own projects (bigquery-public-data, gcp-public-data-- buckets). For BigQuery: 'Google pays for the storage of these datasets... You pay only for the queries that you perform on the data. The first 1 TB per month is free.' For Cloud Storage: 'Google pays for the hosting of these datasets' and they are 'available for users to access for free', including unauthenticated API links. gnomAD and Open Targets are life-science precedents. gnomAD describes its Google-hosted copy as 'fully free to access' in all regions. Open Targets users still saw egress when they downloaded BigQuery data out of the cloud.
mechanisms.userFriction: The lowest possible: anonymous HTTPS for the GCS copies, and the BigQuery sandbox for SQL.
mechanisms.costToUs: $0 for hosting the accepted copy. We'd keep our own bucket as the canonical, hash-pinned source.
mechanisms.costToUser: $0 for GCS access. BigQuery queries beyond 1 TiB/month at $6.25/TiB.
mechanisms.recoversCosts: Better than recovering: Google absorbs the storage and access costs. It covers only data Google accepts, which must be openly distributable, and not the paid tier.
mechanisms.ops: Medium. Apply by email (gcp-public-data@google.com for Cloud Storage, public-data-help@google.com for BigQuery), then keep releases synced to Google's copy. Google's public-datasets-pipelines repository is 'DEPRECATED: this repository is not accepting new PRs', which suggests intake is now curated case by case.
mechanisms.limits: Acceptance criteria, any licence requirement, and whether Google covers internet egress (as opposed to in-cloud access) are not stated in current public docs, so ask Google. 'There is no service-level agreement (SLA) for the Public Dataset Program.' Google controls the hosted copy, so our manifests and sha256 checks would have to verify it. Not suitable for sources marked restricted or non_commercial.

research: GCP mechanisms.notes: WHERE THE FREE/PAID LINE FALLS (recommendation, ordered from least to most friction). Tier 0, anonymous and free: everything published today (observation counts, surfaces, registries, validation evidence) stays on the public bucket and website. At $0.12/GiB, a 0.27 GB release costs about $0.03 per download. The budget covers about 6,000 full downloads a month, and Always Free adds 100 GB of North American egress. Applying to the Public Datasets Program could move this cost to Google. Tier 1, free with a Google sign-in, SQL: the same tables in BigQuery, shared with allAuthenticatedUsers and optionally listed in BigQuery sharing. Queriers pay their own compute, which the 1 TiB/month free tier covers, and the sandbox needs no card. Our storage is under the 10 GiB free tier. Tier 2, paid at cost and billed by Google: a separate Requester Pays bucket for large raw harvests, trained models and bulk products. Google bills each user's own billing account, so we recover 100% of egress and operations with no payments, invoices or tax on our side. The line can also follow size: keep anything up to about 1 GB per object or release free, and put bulk data behind Requester Pays. Tier 3, only if there is demand from users without GCP billing: Identity Platform sign-in (Google and GitHub are free to 50k MAU) plus a Cloud Run signed-URL broker plus prepaid credits through Stripe. This is the only path that bills non-GCP users, and it carries by far the most work. Card fees make charges under about $10 uneconomic. Not recommended: Apigee (environments start at $365/month, and monetization is Subscription-only and still needs a payment processor), Marketplace (Partner Network membership, enterprise-readiness, a PADFA attestation, a 3% fee, flat subscriptions rather than metering), Cloud CDN (pays for itself only above roughly 500 GiB/month), and API Gateway or Endpoints quotas (every consumer needs their own GCP project). KEY CAVEATS. (1) Requester Pays is a per-bucket switch and anonymous reads fail with 400 UserProjectMissing, so the free/paid line is a bucket boundary. Record the tier and bucket per object in the release manifest; fetch_data.py can add --billing-project using only the stdlib (token from gcloud, an ADC refresh, or the metadata server). (2) Any bucket accepts a voluntary billing project, so heavy users can also pay their own way on the free bucket. (3) Load BigQuery data as native tables, or co-locate the dataset with the us-east1 bucket. Otherwise external-table reads bill us inter-region transfer on every query. (4) A shared dataset can have at most 1,000 linked datasets in BigQuery sharing, so also keep direct allAuthenticatedUsers access. (5) ORCID's Public API terms forbid use 'in connection with any revenue-generating product or service', so use ORCID sign-in only for the free tiers unless ORCID agrees. (6) Fees we collect ourselves (Tier 3) may conflict with sources flagged non_commercial in REVIEWED_SOURCES. With Requester Pays, Google charges egress and we charge nothing for the data, which is easier to defend, but have each source's terms checked. (7) Signed URLs are presumably unaffected by the kill switch (they authorize as the signing service account), so a broker needs its own spend cap. (8) Some institution-managed Google accounts can't create projects without their organization, which affects both the sandbox and Requester Pays. NOT VERIFIED (needs a test or a question to Google or ORCID): whether a BigQuery sandbox project can query a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset; whether DuckDB EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS with x-goog-user-project reads a Requester Pays bucket; whether userProject must sit in the signed canonical request for signed URLs on a Requester Pays bucket; whether Identity Platform's OIDC code flow works with ORCID's client_secret_post-only token endpoint; the Public Datasets Program's acceptance criteria and whether it covers internet egress; whether Marketplace data products support usage-based pricing; Apigee subscription pricing. All prices come from Google's live pricing pages, read 2026-10-18 (docs stamped 'Last updated 2026-10-13/15'). The Marketplace revenue-share schedule has been in effect since 2025-04-21. Read-only work: no cloud commands were run, and no repo files were written. Scratch downloads are in <scratchpad>/access-web.

design: leverage.title: Borrow-first access for genomeOS Atlas: sponsors pay for the free tier, users' own cloud accounts pay for the paid tier
design: leverage.summary: The aim is to build as little as possible. Every current dataset stays anonymous and free, exactly as now. Its download cost moves to open-data sponsors that already exist: AWS Open Data Sponsorship, Google Cloud Public Datasets, Hugging Face, and Zenodo for DOIs. That lets the free tier grow without tripping the $200 budget. The "log in and pay at cost" tier is Google's own billing: a separate Requester Pays bucket and a querier-pays BigQuery dataset. The login is the user's Google account. Google bills the user's own billing account, or their institution's, at list price with no markup. genomeOS never takes money and never runs user accounts, passwords, invoices, VAT or a merchant entity. As a result it never charges anyone for data, including non-commercial data. Our cost falls to storage plus a capped free-tier egress. A pure function run by build_data_release.py assigns each object its tier from four inputs: its path class, its bytes, its sources' recorded terms, and whether a sponsor has accepted it. The result is written into the release manifest, and fetch_data.py stays standard-library only. A prepaid-credit broker we would run ourselves (Stripe plus signed URLs) is deferred until users without a cloud account show real demand for at-cost data. The prerequisites that carry the most weight are licences, not code. Project outputs need an open data licence (none is recorded). AFND needs to give written permission (AFND-derived objects are 89% of the bytes in release 2026-10-18), because sponsors require openly licensed data.
design: leverage.tiers:
TIER 0: OPEN, ANONYMOUS, FREE FOREVER (the default, with no sign-in).
- What data: everything published today (registries, observation counts, surfaces in store/artifacts/*/cells.parquet, validation evidence, source records, manifests). This is 248 objects and 271.5 MB in release 2026-10-18. Later, any new object that passes the free rule (freeLine), and any object a sponsor has accepted, whatever its size.
- Who: anyone.
- How they get it:
  - The website, plain HTTPS, scripts/fetch_data.py (standard library, sha256-checked), or DuckDB over HTTP range requests, which reads only the columns and row groups a query needs (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/httpfs/https.html).
  - Hosts, in the order fetch_data.py tries them, are recorded per object in the manifest. Sponsors come first:
    - AWS Open Data Sponsorship (ODP). It covers S3 storage and outbound transfer and requires anonymous access (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
    - A Google Cloud Public Datasets copy. "Google pays for the hosting of these datasets", and they are "available for users to access for free" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/public-datasets).
    - A Hugging Face dataset repo. Free public storage is best-effort, and downloads are rate-limited (3,000 resolver calls per 5 minutes per anonymous IP, 5,000 for a free account), not billed (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-limits, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/rate-limits).
    - Then our own public bucket, https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/.
  - Zenodo holds a citable archive of each release with a DOI (50 GB per record, https://support.zenodo.org/help/en-gb/1-upload-deposit/80-what-are-the-size-limitations-of-zenodo).
  - The hosted P4 read API (Cloud Run) is in this tier too: free, rate-limited per client, viewport-sized responses, and no bulk-export endpoint (bulk means files).
- What it costs them: $0.

TIER 1: OPEN SQL WITH A GOOGLE SIGN-IN (free to us, and usually free to them).
- What data: the same observation, surface and registry tables, loaded per release as native, clustered BigQuery tables.
- Where: a dataset in us-east1, next to the bucket. "There is no charge for batch loading data into BigQuery using the shared slot pool", and a load from a bucket in another location incurs transfer charges (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/batch-loading-data).
- Who: anyone with a Google account. The dataset is shared with allAuthenticatedUsers (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/control-access-to-resources-iam). It is also listed in a public BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub) exchange, where "there's no additional cost for managing data exchanges or listings" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-introduction). If Google's Public Datasets Program accepts it, it is also mirrored in bigquery-public-data, where "Google pays for the storage" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data).
- How: the BigQuery console, the bq CLI or client libraries. The BigQuery sandbox needs no card or billing account (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox).
- What it costs them: the first 1 TiB of query processing a month is free, then $6.25/TiB, with at least 10 MB billed per table referenced (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing). Google bills the querier's project, never us.

TIER 2: AT COST, BILLED BY GOOGLE (needs a login and a billing account).
- What data: objects classed at_cost by the rule. These are large raw third-party harvests (phase 2, #472), trained models once a safe export format exists (#471), and bulk derived products over the free caps that no sponsor hosts.
- Where: a second bucket with Requester Pays turned on (proposed name genomeos-atlas-bulk). The existing bucket is never switched over, because anonymous requests to a Requester Pays bucket fail with 400 UserProjectMissing (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).
- Who: any Google account holding the Service Usage Consumer role on a project with billing enabled (same source).
- How: fetch_data.py --billing-project P. The token comes from an environment variable, the user's ADC refresh token or the metadata server, still standard library only. gcloud storage and DuckDB with an x-goog-user-project header also work (the DuckDB route is not yet tested).
- What it costs them: Google list price, with no markup, on their own bill (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing):
  - $0.12/GiB to the internet (0-10 TiB/month)
  - $0.02/GiB to other North American regions
  - $0 from compute in us-east1
  - $0.0004 per 1,000 Class B reads
- Variant for labs and institutions: the same tier billed to an institutional Google billing account. The institution is invoiced by Google or by a reseller (see the journeys). Institutions on Internet2 NET+, GÉANT/OCRE or reseller contracts can have internet egress waived up to 15% of their monthly Google Cloud fees. Pay-as-you-go accounts are not eligible (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/data-transfer-waiver).

TIER 3: PREPAID CREDITS FOR USERS WITHOUT A CLOUD ACCOUNT (deferred, built only on demand).
- Only if there is evidence of demand: for example, 10 or more distinct requests in a quarter for at_cost objects from users who cannot use a Google account or billing.
- What we would build: Google or GitHub sign-in through Identity Platform (free to 50,000 MAU, https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing), a Cloud Run broker that returns V4 signed URLs (https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls), and Stripe Checkout top-ups with a $10 minimum. Card fees are 2.9% + 30 cents (https://stripe.com/pricing).
- The first response to such demand is to ask a sponsor to take that data class, which makes it Tier 0 instead.
design: leverage.freeLine:
A pure function, genomeos/publication/access_policy.py: tier(object, sources, policy) -> {tier: "open" | "at_cost", hosts: [...]}.
- It is run by build_data_release.py and written into each manifest object.
- Its inputs are only what the manifest already holds (path, bytes, the sources' non_commercial and terms) plus a committed, reviewed data/access-policy.json.
- The policy file holds FREE_CLASSES, OBJECT_CAP = 1 GiB, UNSPONSORED_FREE_CAP = 2 GiB per release, and the sponsor acceptances: host, accepted path prefixes, date and record.

The builder applies these rules in order, and the first match wins.

R1. Restricted terms. If any source has non_commercial = true or terms.status = restricted (today GeneReviews, recorded as restriction_found), the object is open on [gcs-free, hf] only.
- It is never at_cost, never behind any charge or gate, and never on AWS ODP, which refuses licences that limit commercial use (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
- If it would exceed OBJECT_CAP or UNSPONSORED_FREE_CAP, that is a hard build error, and the owner decides (needs-human-decision).

R2. Grandfathered. If the path is in FREE_CLASSES, the object is open, and it can never later become at_cost.
