- FREE_CLASSES are the path classes present in release 2026-10-18, which the owner approved for free distribution: registry/, sources/, raw/afnd_populations.tsv, store/artifacts/, store/catalog-metadata.json, store/INVENTORY.json, validation/ and manifests/.
- Its hosts are the sponsors that accepted it, then gcs-free.

R3. Sponsored. If a sponsor has accepted the object's prefix and the object is sponsor-eligible, it is open with the sponsor host first. Our own GCS copy goes to the Requester Pays bucket, so in-cloud power users pay for their own reads.
- Sponsor-eligible means every source has non_commercial = false and either status explicitly_open or permission_granted, or status no_restriction_found with an open terms.licence recorded (CC0-1.0, CC-BY-4.0 or ODbL).

R4. Small. If bytes <= OBJECT_CAP and the release's running total of open bytes held only on gcs-free stays <= UNSPONSORED_FREE_CAP, the object is open on gcs-free (and on hf when it is sponsor-eligible).

R5. Everything else is at_cost on [gcs-requester-pays].

An object with no valid source, or a status outside the closed vocabulary (explicitly_open, permission_granted, no_restriction_found, restricted, not_checked), is a hard error, never a default.

Operations follow the same line:
- Anonymous GETs and ranged reads of open objects are free.
- P4 API calls are free and rate-limited, and have no bulk endpoint.
- BigQuery SQL is free to us and billed to the querier by Google.
- At-cost reads are billed to the requester's project by Google.
- No operation costs genomeOS anything beyond storage, except anonymous reads served by gcs-free, which the caps bound.

Today's release puts all 248 objects in "open" (R1 for the 6 GeneReviews-linked files, about 316 KB, and R2 for the rest), so nothing currently free changes.
design: leverage.identity:
genomeOS runs no identity system of its own.

- Tiers 0 and 1 (files, mirrors, P4 API): no identity at all, so no account, key, cookie or form.
- Tiers 1 and 2: the "login credential" is the user's Google account. Google enforces it:
  - BigQuery checks allAuthenticatedUsers on the dataset (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/control-access-to-resources-iam).
  - The Requester Pays bucket requires an authenticated request carrying a billing project on which the caller has serviceusage.services.use, the Service Usage Consumer role (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).
- We store no users, emails, passwords or tokens, so there is nothing for us to breach, reset or support.
- Hugging Face tokens are optional and only raise a downloader's rate limit (5,000 to 12,000 resolver calls per 5 minutes, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/rate-limits). Nothing open is gated behind HF login, because ODP forbids gating ("Restricting access by asking for email or contact information is not in line with the program requirements", https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
- We still get usage evidence for funders without asking anyone to register:
  - BigQuery sharing reports jobs and bytes by subscriber project and organization (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-introduction).
  - ODP reviews usage metrics at renewal (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
  - HF shows download counts.
- ORCID sign-in is not used. Its free Public API forbids use "in connection with any revenue-generating product or service" (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/), and its OIDC claims include no email.
- Only if Tier 3 is ever built would we add Identity Platform with the Google and GitHub providers, which are free to 50,000 MAU (https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing).
design: leverage.billing:
genomeOS bills no one.

How each cost is recovered:
- Requester Pays egress and operations go to the requester's own project. "Charges are applied to the billing project supplied in the request." Storage stays with the bucket owner (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).
- BigQuery queries go to the querier's project, with 1 TiB a month free (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).

So recovery of the costs genomeOS incurs per request is exactly 100%, at Google's list price, with:
- no markup
- no payment fees (compared with Stripe's 30-cent fixed fee, 10x the $0.03 cost of a release download, https://stripe.com/pricing)
- no invoicing, sales tax or VAT, refunds or bad debt
- no merchant entity

The owner's "just enough to recoup" is met by construction. What we still pay is storage, plus egress for open objects that only gcs-free serves. Both stay on the existing $200 budget and kill switch (docs/cost-controls.md), and the free caps and the sponsor-first host order bound them. The Requester Pays bucket needs no kill switch, because its egress is not ours.

Ways to lower users' bills, all run by others:
- Google Cloud's $300 trial. It needs a payment method for identity verification (https://cloud.google.com/signup-faqs).
- Google Cloud research credits for faculty, postdocs and PhD students at accredited institutions. They expire 365 days after redemption and cannot be used commercially (https://edu.google.com/programs/credits/research/).
- The education data transfer waiver (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/data-transfer-waiver).
- Reading from compute in us-east1, where same-region transfer is $0 (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).

How institutions pay:
- Google invoiced billing pays by check or wire. It requires at least one year of business registration and expected spend of at least $40,000 a year (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/invoiced-billing). That is why it is an institution-level contract, not a lab one.
- Labs ride on their institution's existing contract, directly with Google or through a reseller. Under NIH STRIDES, for example, a reseller (Carahsoft) invoices against a university PO (https://cloud.nih.gov/, https://kb.wisc.edu/109813).

Fallback: only Tier 3 would make genomeOS a seller. It would use prepaid Stripe Checkout top-ups (no bad debt), with a merchant of record such as Paddle at 5% + 50 cents to absorb international tax (https://www.paddle.com/pricing).
userJourneys:
FIRST-TIME VISITOR (no account, no card, no install).
1. Opens the Atlas site. The map loads anonymously from the web bucket.
2. Clicks a variant. The 'Get the data' panel lists cells.parquet (for example 7.5 MB for the HbS v2 surface) with its sha256, licence, the sources' citations (built from the manifest's sources block) and the release DOI on Zenodo.
3. Clicks Download. The browser GETs the file from the first host in the object's hosts list: the ODP S3 HTTPS URL once AWS accepts the data (AWS pays transfer, https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/), otherwise https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/<key>.
4. Clicks 'Query in browser'. DuckDB-WASM reads only the needed row groups by HTTP range requests (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/httpfs/https.html). Or the visitor copies a one-line read_parquet('https://...') snippet into a local DuckDB.
5. Cites the DOI.
They never see a login, and their cost is $0. Our cost is at most about $0.0008 for that file at $0.12/GiB, inside the 100 GB/month Always Free egress (https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features), and $0 once ODP serves it.

RESEARCHER ON A GPU POD WITHOUT A CLOUD ACCOUNT (for example a rented pod with only Python).
1. Runs git clone --filter=blob:none, then python scripts/fetch_data.py. It is standard library only and pulls the 0.25 GiB open tier anonymously, sponsor host first and GCS as fallback, verifying every sha256 against the committed manifest. A mirror can therefore never substitute bytes.
2. Needs the heavier material: fetch_data.py --prefix raw/ (phase-2 harvests) or the safe-format models. Two cases follow.
3a. The object is open, because a sponsor (ODP or HF) accepted it. It downloads anonymously at $0, at any size. Optionally the researcher sets HF_TOKEN from a free HF account to raise the rate limit (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/rate-limits).
3b. The object is at_cost. fetch_data.py stops before downloading and prints the bytes, the exact cost at Google list price (for example 23 GiB x $0.12 = $2.76 to the internet, https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing), and three ways to pay:
- On a laptop, create a Google Cloud project. The $300 trial needs a payment method for verification (https://cloud.google.com/signup-faqs). Run gcloud auth print-access-token and paste the token into GENOMEOS_GCS_TOKEN on the pod. It lasts one hour (https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/token-types). Then run fetch_data.py --billing-project <project>.
- Ask the PI for the Service Usage Consumer role on the lab's billing project (see the lab journey).
- Apply for Google research credits (https://edu.google.com/programs/credits/research/).
4. No genomeOS account is created at any point, and genomeOS sees no money.

HEAVY SQL USER.
1. Opens the BigQuery console with any Google account and creates a sandbox project (no card, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox).
2. Queries `<atlas-project>.atlas_2026_10_18.surface_cells` directly (allAuthenticatedUsers read), or clicks Subscribe on the public BigQuery sharing listing to get a linked dataset in their own project (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-introduction). If Google accepts the data into bigquery-public-data, it is that path instead. Whether a sandbox can read a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset needs a test before launch.
3. Tables are clustered by variant_id and H3 parent, so a typical query scans megabytes. The 1 TiB/month free tier covers roughly 110,000 minimum-size (10 MB) queries (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).
4. Past 1 TiB, they enable billing on their project and pay $6.25/TiB on their own bill. For example, 3 TiB a month costs $12.50.
5. For joins against their own large data, they either stay in BigQuery or move to local DuckDB over the open Parquet, which is free and anonymous.
We pay only BigQuery storage, which is inside the first free 10 GiB today.

LAB PAYING BY INVOICE.
1. The PI asks research computing for a Google Cloud project on the institution's billing account. Universities usually procure Google Cloud through a contract and reseller rather than a card. Under NIH STRIDES, for example, the researcher fills in a reseller billing-account form, the university issues a PO against the reseller's quote, and the reseller invoices (https://kb.wisc.edu/109813, https://cloud.nih.gov/). Internet2 NET+ is the US higher-education route (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/data-transfer-waiver).
2. IT grants lab members Service Usage Consumer (for Requester Pays) and BigQuery Job User on the lab project, and sets a budget alert on it.
3. Members run fetch_data.py --billing-project <lab-project> for at_cost objects, and BigQuery jobs billed to that project.
4. Charges appear on the institution's monthly Google or reseller invoice, paid by PO, check or wire. If the institution has the Internet2, GÉANT or reseller data transfer waiver, internet egress is waived up to 15% of its monthly Google Cloud fees (same source).
5. genomeOS issues no quote, invoice or W-9 and keeps no ledger. A lab with no cloud contract that insists on a genomeOS invoice is the demand signal that would justify Tier 3 (Stripe Invoicing at 0.4% per paid invoice, https://stripe.com/invoicing/pricing).
design: leverage.costModel:
Assumptions:
- Release 2026-10-18 is 271,494,507 bytes (0.2528 GiB). It carries forward unchanged keys from 2026-10-17, so releases deduplicate.
- Today's traffic is not measured. I assume about 200 full downloads a month.
- Prices from https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing: GCS egress $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB a month, Standard storage about $0.02/GiB-month in us-east1.
- Always Free: 100 GB of egress from North America, 5 GB-month of storage and 50,000 Class B operations a month (https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features).
- BigQuery (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing): storage free for the first 10 GiB, then about $0.023/GiB-month active; queries $6.25/TiB after 1 TiB a month free; loads free (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/batch-loading-data).
- The website bucket is out of scope.

NOW, for us: about $0 a month.
- Storage is about 0.3 GB, inside the 5 GB-month free tier.
- 200 full downloads are 50.6 GiB, inside the 100 GB free tier (about 368 full downloads). Each further full download costs $0.03.
- The $200 budget covers about 6,960 full downloads a month. The $300 kill switch trips at about 10,250.
- BigQuery tables are under 1 GiB: storage free, loads free.
- The Requester Pays bucket is empty.
- Sponsor mirrors cost $0. ODP pays storage and egress, and the ODP-only AWS account is placed in AWS's billing organization (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/open-data-sponsorship-program/).

NOW, for users: $0 for everyone, because everything published today is open.

AT 100x TRAFFIC (about 20,000 full downloads a month, 5,057 GiB):
- Status quo, with GCS only: (5,057 - 93 free) x $0.12 = about $596 a month. The kill switch would trip around mid-month and take the free tier offline.
- With the sponsor-first host order, if 95% of fetches are served by ODP or HF, our GCS share is about 253 GiB, which is about $19 a month. At 90% it is about $50.
- The free tier also survives a kill-switch trip, because the sponsor copies keep serving.
- Users still pay $0.

AT 100x DATA (a release of about 27 GB: at most 2 GiB open on GCS, about 23 GiB of harvests and models):
- Storage: with about 12 retained releases and half the bytes new each time, about 175 GB, so about $3.50 a month. BigQuery: about 75 GiB across three live releases, about $1.50 a month. Total about $5 a month for us, plus the capped free-tier egress above.
- Users who fetch the at_cost set pay Google for their own transfer:
  - $2.76 per 23 GiB full download to the internet
  - $0.46 to another North American region
  - $0 from us-east1 compute
  - possibly $0 under an education egress waiver
- If ODP accepts that class, it costs everyone $0.
- Heavy SQL: typical clustered queries stay in the free 1 TiB. A 3 TiB-a-month user pays $12.50.

AT BOTH (100x users and 100x data), with sponsors: about $25-60 a month for us, inside the $200 budget, with $0 of payment-processing cost. Without sponsors, the free tier's egress alone exceeds the budget. Getting a sponsor is therefore the most important single step.

Tier 3, if ever built, costs about 5.9% of every $10 top-up in card fees ($0.59, https://stripe.com/pricing), plus our own ledger and support. That is why it is deferred.
design: leverage.terms:
What release 2026-10-18 records, per source (data/releases/2026-10-18.json), and what each means under this design:

- cpic: CC0-1.0, no_restriction_found. Any tier and any sponsor.
- clinvar: no_restriction_found. ClinVar asks that copied or distributed data be attributed to it. Free or at cost; sponsor-eligible once a licence or permission is recorded; attribution must travel.
- map: no_restriction_found. MAP's open-access policy asks users to cite the original sources, and the owner approved redistribution on 2026-10-18. Attribution must travel. Sponsors need an open licence, so ask MAP whether its policy counts, or get written permission (permission_granted).
- afnd: no_restriction_found, but no licence. It is a source of 113 objects, 242 MB, or 89% of the release's bytes, including 56 surface artifacts. AWS ODP requires openly licensed data and "recommends CC BY 4.0" (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/). These objects stay free on GCS and HF, but are not sponsor-eligible until AFND gives written permission.
- worldpop: recorded as not_checked. WorldPop states its datasets are CC BY 4.0 (https://hub.worldpop.org/). Record the check, and attribution must travel.
- genomeos (project-authored, 103 objects): not_checked, with no data licence. Apache-2.0 covers code only. The owner should choose a data licence (CC BY 4.0, which ODP recommends) before any sponsor application.
- genereviews: non_commercial = true, status restriction_found (6 registry files, about 316 KB, holding links only). Rule R1 applies: always free and anonymous, never behind any charge, never on ODP.

How charging interacts with these terms:
- In Tiers 0-2, genomeOS receives no money. The only charges are Google's list prices for transport and compute, billed by Google to the user's own account (Requester Pays, BigQuery).
- That is the strongest position available under CC BY-NC-style terms, which define non-commercial as "not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation" (https://wiki.creativecommons.org/NonCommercial_interpretation).
- Even so, R1 keeps non_commercial material off every charged or gated path. So the question of whether cost recovery counts as commercial never has to be answered for GeneReviews or for the field-level restrictions in genomeos/publication/commercial_use.py (gnomad.spliceai and alphagenome.top_attributions, neither published today).
- If Tier 3 is ever built, genomeos would then be collecting money. In that case the at_cost price list is computed only over objects whose sources are all non_commercial = false, and R1 still applies.

Attribution:
- mirror_release.py writes an ATTRIBUTION.md, generated from the manifest's sources block (names, citations, terms URLs), beside every mirrored release.
- BigQuery table and listing descriptions carry the same text.
- The mirror script refuses to copy an object without its attribution record.

Two fixes:
- ORCID is not used, so ORCID's ban on use with revenue-generating services does not arise.
- The repository has a vocabulary gap. data_release.py accepts any non-empty terms.status, and GeneReviews uses restriction_found while commercial_use.py's closed list uses restricted. The tier function must not rely on a free-form string, so close the vocabulary and treat non_commercial = true as authoritative.
build:
PR 1, terms groundwork (code plus owner and outreach steps).
- Close terms.status in genomeos/publication/data_release.py to the five values in commercial_use.COMMERCIAL_USE_FINDINGS. Accept the legacy restriction_found only when reading old immutable manifests, and map it to restricted in new builds.
- Record the WorldPop CC BY 4.0 check in REVIEWED_SOURCES.
- Owner decision: a data licence for project outputs (recommend CC BY 4.0).
- Outreach: email AFND and MAP for written permission covering redistribution of derived surfaces by third-party mirrors.
- Tests for the vocabulary.

PR 2, the access policy and tier function.
- Add genomeos/publication/access_policy.py: a pure function with no HTTP that implements rules R1-R5.
- Add data/access-policy.json: FREE_CLASSES, a 1 GiB object cap, a 2 GiB unsponsored cap, the host table, and sponsor acceptances (empty at first).
- Manifest schema_version 2 adds a per-object access block {tier, hosts}. build_data_release.py fills it in, and an unclassifiable object or unknown status is a hard error.
- A CI check fails a release whose open bytes held only on gcs-free exceed the cap.
- Tests: today's release classifies as all open, and the GeneReviews files are R1.

PR 3, multi-host fetch.
- scripts/fetch_data.py reads each object's hosts and tries them in order.
- Mirror base URLs are committed constants, which amends data store design C8. A fetch still refuses any other URL.
- The manifest is read only from git or the GCS manifests/ key, never from a mirror, and sha256 is verified as now.
- New flags: --host to pin one host, and a cost preview for at_cost objects. Still standard library only.
- Tests use a loopback server for each host.

PR 4, sponsor mirrors (the owner applies first).
- Owner applies to AWS ODP (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/open-data-sponsorship-program/; decisions generally within two weeks; requires a new AWS account used only for hosting).
- Owner emails gcp-public-data@google.com (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/public-datasets) and bq-public-data@google.com (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data).
- Move the interim HF mirror to an organisation-owned public dataset.
- Then the code: scripts/mirror_release.py copies sponsor-eligible objects per host, verifies sha256 after copy, writes ATTRIBUTION.md, and records each acceptance in access-policy.json. Also a Zenodo deposit per citable release, with its DOI added to the manifest, and the Registry of Open Data YAML submitted as its own PR upstream.

PR 5, open SQL in BigQuery.
- scripts/publish_bigquery.py loads each release's observation, surface and registry Parquet into native tables in a us-east1 dataset: free loads, no cross-region transfer. Tables are clustered by variant_id and H3 parent, and descriptions carry the citations and terms.
- scripts/provision_bigquery_public.py (an owner step) grants allAuthenticatedUsers read and creates the BigQuery sharing exchange and listing.
- Before announcing: a manual test that a sandbox project can query the dataset.

PR 6, the at-cost bucket.
- Extend scripts/provision_data_store_bucket.py with --tier at-cost: Requester Pays on, allAuthenticatedUsers read, no listing, same publisher role. The owner runs it.
- publish_data_store.py routes at_cost objects to that bucket.
- fetch_data.py gains --billing-project, with a standard-library token from GENOMEOS_GCS_TOKEN, the authorized_user ADC refresh token, or the metadata server.
- Test DuckDB EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS with x-goog-user-project, and document the result.

PR 7, the 'Get the data' surface.
- Add docs/access.md and a website panel: the tier ladder, each file's size, host and at-cost price computed from the manifest, plus DuckDB, BigQuery and fetch_data snippets.
- Links to the BigQuery sandbox, research credits, the education egress waiver and institutional procurement.
- The 'cite' button uses the Zenodo DOI.

PR 8, a demand gate for Tier 3 (docs only).
- An issue template, 'I need at-cost data without a cloud account', with the label needs-human-decision, plus a stated threshold (for example 10 distinct requesters in a quarter).
- Tier 3 (Identity Platform, signed-URL broker, Stripe Checkout) is designed and built only once the threshold is met, and first we ask a sponsor to take the class instead.
risks: Sponsorship is discretionary and can end. ODP reviews usage at renewal (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/). Google's program has no SLA and no published intake criteria (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data). Azure dropped gnomAD's genomic datasets in 2025 (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/news/2025-07-azure-open-datasets-deprecation). Mitigation: GCS stays the source of truth, mirrors are only additive, and the manifest and sha256 make any mirror replaceable.

Licence gaps may block the sponsors. Project outputs have no data licence, AFND has none (89% of current bytes), and the repo records WorldPop as not_checked. If AFND does not answer, the bulk of today's data stays on our own egress budget.

Requester Pays friction is real. Even the $300 trial needs a payment method (https://cloud.google.com/signup-faqs), and some institution-managed Google accounts cannot create projects. Users without a cloud account who need at_cost objects are blocked until a sponsor takes that class or Tier 3 exists.
Without a sponsor, 100x traffic means about $596 a month of free-tier egress, which trips the kill switch. The caps in R4 limit how big the free set can grow, but not how often it is downloaded.

Several things are unverified and need tests:
- whether a BigQuery sandbox can query a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset or subscribe to a sharing listing
- whether DuckDB's x-goog-user-project header works against a Requester Pays bucket
- whether Google's Public Datasets GCS copy also covers internet egress, not just in-cloud access
- whether Google bills for responses served from its edge cache (already open in docs/cost-controls.md)
Amending C8 (a single committed URL) widens what fetch_data.py trusts. This stays safe only while the manifest is never read from a mirror, and a test must enforce that.

Copies can drift. Mirrors, BigQuery tables and Zenodo can disagree with GCS if a sync fails halfway. mirror_release.py must verify after copying, and fetch_data.py must keep hard-failing on a hash mismatch.
Policy drift: someone could raise the caps or add a FREE_CLASS to make a release pass. access-policy.json therefore changes only by a reviewed PR, like the 150% kill-switch constant.

Recovery is incomplete for anyone outside Google Cloud. 'Recoup' covers only users who can bill Google. If many users without a cloud account need at_cost data, we either absorb their egress or build Tier 3, which brings the very ops, tax and non-commercial-terms exposure this design avoids.

Storage of at_cost objects is never recovered (the bucket owner always pays storage). It is about $0.02/GiB-month, so a 1 TB archive is about $20 a month (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing). Prune old releases from BigQuery and keep at_cost objects deduplicated across releases.
whyNotOthers: Building our own login, metering and Stripe billing now: it is the only option that bills users without a cloud account, but it has the most ops (a ledger, refunds, receipts, VAT or a merchant of record, abuse handling, a spend cap for signed URLs). Stripe's fixed 30-cent fee is about 10x a $0.03 release download (https://stripe.com/pricing). It also makes genomeOS the party collecting money, which is the worst position under non-commercial terms. It is deferred behind a demand gate.

Google Cloud Marketplace data product: it requires Partner Network membership, enterprise readiness and a business-case review (https://cloud.google.com/marketplace/docs/partners/get-started), a 3% revenue share (https://cloud.google.com/terms/marketplace-revenue-share-schedule), and an attestation about sensitive data under a statute that lists genetic information (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/9901). The documented pricing models are flat subscriptions, not per-query or per-download recovery (https://docs.cloud.google.com/marketplace/docs/partners/data).

Apigee monetization: pay-as-you-go environments start at $365 a month per region (https://cloud.google.com/apigee/pricing), above the whole budget. Monetization is subscription-only and still leaves invoicing to us (https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/monetization/overview).

API Gateway or Endpoints quotas: they meter and throttle, but bill no one, and every consumer needs its own Google Cloud project and API key (https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/quotas-overview).

Turning on Requester Pays for the existing bucket: anonymous requests would then fail with 400 UserProjectMissing (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays). That ends the free anonymous tier the owner requires, and it breaks every published link and the standard-library fetch.

Cloud CDN in front of the free bucket: a forwarding rule costs about $18 a month whatever the traffic, and CDN only pays for itself above roughly 500 GiB a month (https://cloud.google.com/cdn/pricing). A sponsor mirror removes the egress outright, at $0.

A login wall on the free data (HF gated datasets, GBIF-style accounts, an OpenAlex-style key): every step down the friction ladder loses users, and gating disqualifies the data from AWS ODP (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/). Throttling (the P4 API) and sponsor hosting control abuse without a wall.

ORCID sign-in: the free Public API may not be used 'in connection with any revenue-generating product or service' (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/). The paid alternative is a membership fee, and ORCID's claims include no email.

A second paid cloud (AWS Data Exchange, or an S3 Requester Pays mirror): ADX can put transfer costs on subscribers with Requester Pays (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/data-exchange/latest/userguide/subscribing-to-S3-data-access.html). But it doubles the paid-tier operations, and AWS users already get every open object free through ODP. Revisit only if AWS-only labs ask for at_cost data.

Running a platform like Terra/AnVIL or UK Biobank's RAP: these are analysis-in-place environments for controlled individual-level data (https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/), far heavier than open aggregate counts need. A demo Terra workspace that reads our buckets is the most we would ever add.

Relying only on Source Cooperative or Hugging Face: Source Cooperative's pricing is still 'announced soon' (https://source.coop/), and HF's free public storage is best-effort (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-limits). Both are good mirrors but not the only home, which is why GCS stays canonical and ODP is the main sponsor to pursue.

design: friction.title: Open by default, pay at cost by exception: least-friction tiered access for genomeOS Atlas
design: friction.summary: Angle: least friction first. Nobody signs in to explore or download anything that is cheap for us to serve. The first paid step is one GitHub or Google sign-in plus a single prepaid top-up, with no cloud account. Nobody can be billed more than they agreed to beforehand. Five rungs: (0) Open: anonymous, $0, unchanged from today. Every object in release 2026-10-18 stays here (248 objects, 271,494,507 bytes; the largest is a 7.5 MB cells.parquet). Two additions: a zero-egress Hugging Face mirror, so the free tier survives a kill-switch trip and scales to 100x, and SQL over the same Parquet with DuckDB in the browser or CLI. (1) Signed in, still $0: one click with GitHub or Google and no card. This gives an API key, a device-code login for headless pods, and a $1/month allowance for metered objects. The allowances draw on a global pool capped at $50/month. (2) Prepaid pay-as-you-go: top-ups of at least $10 through a merchant of record. Metered downloads cost list egress plus payment fees ($0.135/GiB against GCS's $0.12). Every charge is quoted first, and access stops hard at a zero balance. (3) Teams: the same prices, but a prepaid credit block bought by quote, PO and invoice, with a shared wallet and a cap per member. Beside the ladder, not on it, runs a bring-your-own-cloud lane: a BigQuery dataset shared with allAuthenticatedUsers (BigQuery sandbox, no card, 1 TiB/month free) and a Requester Pays copy of the metered objects. Google bills those users directly and we take no money. The free/paid line is a rule the release builder applies to each object and records in the manifest (schema v2). Data is free when one download costs us 12¢ or less (1 GiB from GCS, any size on a zero-egress mirror), or when it belongs to one of today's dataset classes. It may be metered only if every source has a performed terms check that allows it: never for non_commercial, restricted or not_checked sources. Under that rule, every surface (WorldPop input, not_checked) and every project-authored output (no data licence recorded) can be free but not metered. Recording those two terms is a prerequisite for ever charging for models. Our cost today is about $0-2/month. At 100x with the mirror it is about $100/month net, and about $240/month without the mirror, which is over the $200 budget. Metered traffic belongs in a second GCP project, or paid downloads would trip the free tier's kill switch.
design: friction.tiers:
TIER 0 — OPEN (anonymous, $0, forever).
- What: every object the rule marks `open`. Today that is all 248 objects of release 2026-10-18: registries, observation counts (ac/an), surfaces (cells.parquet), validation evidence, curated sources, catalog metadata and manifests.
- Who: anyone.
- How:
  - The Atlas website, served from the web bucket.
  - Plain HTTPS GETs on https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/<key>.
  - scripts/fetch_data.py, which needs only the standard library. New: HF mirror first, GCS fallback, the same sha256 checks against the committed manifest.
  - DuckDB over HTTP range reads, which fetch only the needed columns and row groups (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/httpfs/https.html), in the CLI, in Python, or in the browser through DuckDB-WASM on the Atlas site.
  - Bounded API lookups (one variant, one cell, a tile, the catalog) with a rate limit per IP.
- Cost to them: $0. No sign-in prompt appears anywhere on open data.

TIER 1 — SIGNED IN, STILL $0 (one click, no card).
- What: everything in Tier 0, plus the following.
  - An API key, or a device-code login for pods and CI.
  - A $1.00/month allowance spent on metered objects and metered queries, about 7.4 GiB at $0.135/GiB. Allowances draw on a global pool capped at $50/month; if the pool runs out, allowances pause until the 1st and the site says so.
  - Higher rate limits on the hosted API, if the parallel query design ships one.
  - A download history that carries each object's citations.
- Who: anyone with a GitHub or Google account. These count as "Social" providers, free to 50,000 MAU (https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing).
- Cost to them: $0. No card is ever stored at this tier.

TIER 2 — PREPAID PAY-AS-YOU-GO (one sign-in plus one checkout; no cloud account).
- What: `metered` objects, and queries beyond the allowance.
- How:
  - A checkout through a merchant of record, by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay. Minimum top-up $10; Paddle needs bespoke pricing below $10 (https://www.paddle.com/pricing).
  - The broker quotes each request, debits the ledger, then returns 15-minute V4 signed URLs. Bytes flow straight from GCS (https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls).
- Cost to them:
  - Transfer at list price divided by 0.89: $0.12/GiB becomes $0.135/GiB, which covers fees of up to about 11%.
  - Compute at Cloud Run list price divided by 0.89.
  - Storage is never charged.
- No-surprise rules:
  - Prices are shown in dollars, not credits.
  - Every charge is quoted and confirmed before it happens (`--max-spend` in the CLI, the price on the button on the site).
  - Each key has a monthly cap, $10 by default.
  - Auto-recharge is off unless opted in.
  - At a zero balance the broker returns HTTP 402 with a top-up link. There is never an overage.
  - Unused balance is refundable on request and valid for 24 months after the last top-up.

TIER 3 — TEAMS AND INSTITUTIONS (the same prices, paid by invoice).
- What: everything in Tier 2, from a shared team wallet.
- How:
  - A PI requests a quote for a prepaid block ($250, $500 or $2,000).
  - An invoice carrying the institution's PO number, payable by bank transfer or card on net terms. Paddle's manually collected transactions carry a PO number and payment terms (https://developer.paddle.com/build/invoices/create-issue-invoices/). Alternative: Stripe Invoicing at 0.4% per paid invoice (https://stripe.com/invoicing/pricing).
  - Members join by GitHub login or verified email, and the PI sets a monthly cap for each member.
  - A monthly statement CSV, per member and per object, with citations, for grant reporting.
- Cost to them: the block price. Fees are absorbed by the same 11% margin. There are never overage invoices.

LANE C — BRING YOUR OWN CLOUD (parallel and optional; zero markup; we collect nothing).
- BigQuery dataset shared with allAuthenticatedUsers:
  - The querier's project pays and the owner does not (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).
  - The sandbox needs no card or billing account (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox).
  - The first 1 TiB/month is free, then $6.25/TiB.
- A Requester Pays bucket holding the metered objects:
  - The requester pays operations and egress (https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays): $0.12/GiB to the internet, $0 into us-east1 compute.
  - fetch_data.py gets a `--billing-project` flag, which also works voluntarily on the free bucket.
- Who: users who already have GCP. Cost to them: Google list price, billed by Google.
design: friction.freeLine:
Principle: an object is free when one download of it costs us less than any charge we could collect, or when it belongs to a class the owner has promised to keep free. It may be charged for only if every one of its sources has a performed terms check that allows charging. The release builder (scripts/build_data_release.py) applies the rule, writes `access` ∈ {open, metered, byo_cloud} into every manifest object (schema_version 2), and stops with a hard error on anything it cannot place. Fetchers, the broker and the website read `access` from the manifest. They never infer it.

CONSTANTS (committed in genomeos/publication/data_release.py; changed only by a reviewed PR):
- EGRESS_USD_PER_GIB = 0.12. GCS internet egress for 0–10 TiB (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).
- OPEN_FETCH_COST_MAX_USD = 0.12. One download costs at most 12¢, which means at most 1 GiB from GCS. The cheapest charge we can collect, a $10 card top-up, loses 59¢ to fees (2.9% + 30¢, https://stripe.com/pricing), so billing anything below this costs more than it recovers.
- OPEN_CLASSES = the INCLUDE roots of release 2026-10-18 plus manifests/: registry/, sources/, raw/afnd_populations.tsv, store/artifacts/ (observations and surfaces), store/catalog-metadata.json, store/INVENTORY.json, validation/.
- OPEN_RELEASE_GCS_GIB_MAX = 10. A full free download of a release costs at most $1.20.
- CHARGEABLE = {explicitly_open, permission_granted, no_restriction_found}. This is an allowlist, so the release vocabulary (restriction_found) and the web vocabulary (restricted) are both blocked, and so is any status added later.
- MIRRORS = the committed anonymous mirrors with their egress cost to us. For example, the existing public Hugging Face dataset costs us $0.

RULE (the first rule that matches wins):
- R1 Override. An entry in ACCESS_OVERRIDES (path prefix → access, reason, issue URL) decides. It can never set `metered` on an object that R2 forbids.
- R2 Terms. If any source of the object has non_commercial = true, or a terms status outside CHARGEABLE, the object is never metered. It is `open` if R3 or R4 admits it. Otherwise the build fails with: "too large to be free and its terms forbid charging; add a zero-egress mirror, split the restricted fields into their own object, or add a byo_cloud override (Google bills the user and we receive nothing)."
- R3 Class. A path under OPEN_CLASSES is `open` at any size. This keeps the owner's promise that today's datasets stay free.
- R4 Cost. If bytes / 2^30 × the cheapest egress among GCS and the mirrors that hold the object is at most OPEN_FETCH_COST_MAX_USD, the object is `open`. So any object on a $0 mirror is free whatever its size.
- R5 Otherwise the object is `metered`. It is served through the broker, and it is also copied into the Requester Pays bucket and, if it is tabular, BigQuery.

RELEASE CHECK: the `open` objects served only from GCS must total at most OPEN_RELEASE_GCS_GIB_MAX, or the build fails.

OPERATIONS:
- A bounded read (one variant, cell, tile or catalog page, with a response of at most 10 MB) is open and anonymous, with a rate limit per IP.
- An unbounded operation (ad-hoc SQL, scans, bulk export) on our compute needs a key and is priced at measured cost. It is estimated beforehand and refused before it runs if the allowance plus the balance cannot cover it.
- SQL in client-side DuckDB or in BigQuery uses no compute of ours, so it is never metered.

APPLIED TODAY: all 248 objects are open by R3, and R4 would admit them too.

PHASE 2 (#472):
- WorldPop's 1 km tif (about 870 MB) is open by R4, and as not_checked it can never be metered.
- The gnomAD and AlphaGenome caches are open while each object stays at or under 1 GiB. Their SpliceAI and top_attributions fields must ship as separate objects so the permissive remainder can be metered if it grows.
- Exported fits (#471) carry genomeos and worldpop sources, both not_checked, so they stay free-only until the owner records a data licence and a WorldPop terms check.
design: friction.identity:
Tier 0 needs no identity at all: no account, cookie, token or key.

Tiers 1–3:
- Sign-in uses Firebase Authentication on Identity Platform, with Google and GitHub as providers.
  - Tier 1 "Social" sign-ins are free for the first 50,000 MAU, then $0.0055/MAU (https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing).
  - There are no passwords, so there are no reset or breach flows.
- Accounts are keyed by the Firebase uid. We store the provider and an email address for receipts, and nothing else.
- The website uses the Firebase JS SDK popup. The broker verifies Firebase ID tokens on every account call.

Headless use (GPU pods, CI):
- Either paste a key into GENOMEOS_API_KEY, or run `fetch_data.py login`, a device-authorization flow in the RFC 8628 shape that the broker implements.
- The CLI prints <site>/device and an 8-character code, then polls. The user approves on a laptop or phone, signed in through Firebase.
- This copies the UX GitHub documents for its own device flow (8-character code, 15-minute expiry, minimum polling interval; https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps).
- Google's own device flow allows only the openid, email and profile scopes (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/limited-input-device), which would also be enough. One flow of our own covers both providers.

API keys:
- 256 random bits, prefixed `gos_` so secret scanners can match them, shown once and stored as SHA-256.
- Each key is named after its device and carries scopes (download, query) and a monthly spend cap ($10 by default).
- Keys can be revoked on the account page. The CLI stores its key in ~/.config/genomeos/credentials with mode 0600.

Teams: an owner plus members invited by GitHub login or verified email. Never grant team or institutional rights by email domain alone. A JupyterHub CILogon authenticator advisory found it checked only the email address, not which provider issued it (https://www.miggo.io/vulnerability-database/cve/CVE-2022-31027).

ORCID is not used at launch:
- Its Public API terms forbid use "in connection with any revenue-generating product or service" (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/).
- Its OIDC claims carry no email.
- Later, "link your ORCID iD" for attribution only, once ORCID confirms that is acceptable next to a cost-recovery service, or with paid membership.

Lane C uses the user's own Google identity and project. We see it only in our audit logs.

Privacy: download logs show which variants a researcher is studying. Keep rows per object only for statements, for 13 months, use no third-party analytics, and publish a short privacy notice.
design: friction.billing:
Prepaid only, priced in dollars, at cost plus payment fees. No subscriptions, no postpaid metering, no automatic recharge unless the user opts in.

PRICING (genomeos/access/pricing.py, versioned and reviewed by diff; pure, with no HTTP, per AGENTS.md):
- price = list cost / (1 − 0.11).
- Transfer: $0.12/GiB becomes $0.135/GiB. Metered objects are charged for their full size once per issued URL, so the price is predictable even when reads are ranged.
- Compute: Cloud Run list rates divided by 0.89.
- Storage is never charged; we absorb it at about $0.02/GiB-month.
- The 11% margin covers the worst merchant-of-record case on a $10 top-up:
  - Stripe Managed Payments is standard Stripe fees plus 3.5%, about $0.94 on $10 and $1.09 with an international card (https://stripe.com/managed-payments, https://stripe.com/pricing).
  - Paddle is 5% + 50¢, so $1.00 on $10 (https://www.paddle.com/pricing).

COLLECTION: through a merchant of record, because a seller outside the EU owes EU VAT on electronic services to consumers from the first sale, with no threshold (https://vat-one-stop-shop.ec.europa.eu/one-stop-shop_en). A merchant of record files that tax for us.
- Stripe Managed Payments accepts US-based businesses selling "Electronically Delivered Information Services". It excludes data brokering, requires that "you hold all necessary rights and licenses to distribute the product", and does not support one-off invoices (https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/eligibility, https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments).
- Paddle covers both checkout and invoices with a PO number under one merchant of record, so it is the default. Stripe Managed Payments is the fallback for card top-ups. Either one requires the provider's eligibility review.

LEDGER:
- Firestore, append-only: topup, debit, refund, reissue and allowance entries. The balance is their sum.
- Each debit is idempotent on (key, quote_id, object) and is written before the signed URL is issued.
- At our size it fits Firestore's free quota of 50,000 reads and 20,000 writes per day (https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/quotas).

FLOW: quote → confirm (`--max-spend`, or a button showing the price) → debit → URL.
- At a zero balance, HTTP 402 with a top-up link.
- Emails at 50%, 80% and 100% of a key's cap or a team's block.
- A paid object can be re-issued twice within 7 days at no charge, which covers interrupted downloads.

ALLOWANCE: $1/month per account, spent before the balance, from a pool capped at $50/month.

ISOLATION: the metered bucket, the broker, Identity Platform and the ledger live in a second GCP project (its id is never committed), with alert-only budgets.
- The existing $200 budget and its kill switch cover the free tier only. Budgets are scoped by project (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets).
- Our worst-case unrecovered spend per month is the allowance pool. The broker never issues a URL that is not covered by a prepaid balance or the pool.

RECONCILIATION: a monthly job compares the billing export (already described in docs/cost-controls.md) with ledger revenue and publishes a cost-recovery report. If recovery stays above 105% for a quarter, the price comes down; below 95%, it goes up. Either change is a PR.

LANE C: Google bills the user directly, and we never see money.
userJourneys:
FIRST-TIME VISITOR (never signs in).
1. Opens the Atlas site. The map renders from the web bucket (about 0.5–4 MB of tiers per view, by the fast-load design), with no sign-in prompt and no cookie wall.
2. Clicks HbS. The Download panel lists cells.parquet (7.5 MB), the observations and the manifest. Each entry shows its size, its sha256, a citation block copied from the manifest's sources (MAP: Piel 2013 and Howes 2012; WorldPop), and the label "free, no account".
3. Clicks "Query in your browser". A DuckDB-WASM SQL box opens with example queries over the open Parquet. Only the needed byte ranges are fetched.
4. Clicks "Get everything". The page shows `curl -LO <release>/fetch_data.pyz && python3 fetch_data.pyz`, a single-file stdlib fetcher, or the git-clone route. 271 MB download and are checked against the committed manifest.
5. If a later release holds a metered object, its panel shows the price before anything else, for example "42.1 GiB · $5.69 · sign in to use your free $1 allowance or top up". Nothing is charged, and nothing asks for a card, until the visitor chooses to.

RESEARCHER ON A GPU POD WITH NO CLOUD ACCOUNT.
1. On the pod, runs `git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/genomeOS/genomeOS && python3 scripts/fetch_data.py`. Open objects stream anonymously, from the HF mirror first with GCS as the fallback, and are sha256-checked. The standard library is enough.
2. Asks for a metered harvest: `python3 scripts/fetch_data.py --prefix raw/<harvest>/`. The script downloads nothing. It prints "3 metered objects, 42.1 GiB, $5.69. Not signed in: run `fetch_data.py login` or set GENOMEOS_API_KEY" and exits with status 3.
3. Runs `python3 scripts/fetch_data.py login`. It prints <site>/device and the code WDJB-MJHT, then polls.
4. On a laptop or phone, opens the link, signs in with GitHub in one click, and approves the device "runpod-a100-1" with the scopes download and query and a default cap of $10/month.
5. The CLI saves the key to ~/.config/genomeos/credentials (mode 0600). Alternatively, the researcher pastes a key into the pod's secrets as GENOMEOS_API_KEY.
6. Re-runs the fetch. It prints "Quote $5.69: allowance $1.00, balance $0.00, $4.69 short" and a top-up link. The researcher pays $10 by Apple Pay on the phone in about 30 seconds.
7. Runs `fetch_data.py --prefix raw/<harvest>/ --max-spend 6`. For each object the broker debits the ledger and returns a 15-minute signed URL. Bytes come straight from GCS and are sha256-checked against the manifest. A receipt listing each object and its citations is printed and emailed. Balance left: $5.31.
8. The pod is pre-empted halfway through. Re-running within 7 days re-issues URLs for objects already paid for, at no charge (two re-issues each). Nothing is ever charged twice and there is never an overage.

HEAVY SQL USER.
1. With no sign-in, in DuckDB: `INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<release>/store/artifacts/*/cells.parquet') WHERE ...;` with the keys taken from the manifest. Column and row-group pruning keep the egress small, and it costs the user nothing.
2. For joins across every variant and release, or against their own BigQuery tables: signs in to the Google Cloud console and creates a sandbox project, with no card. Then runs `SELECT ... FROM <genomeos-project>.atlas_<release>.cells`. Queries are billed to the querier's project and the first 1 TiB/month is free. A sandbox cannot be billed, so at the cap queries simply fail until the next month.
3. Beyond 1 TiB, the user attaches their own billing ($6.25/TiB). The docs recommend first setting the QueryUsagePerDay custom quota, which refuses a query in advance if it would exceed the quota (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/custom-quotas), and a budget on their own project.
4. Metered tables are in BigQuery too. Querying them costs us only storage, so the user pays nothing to us. Metering applies only to downloads that leave our project at our expense.
5. If the parallel design ships a hosted SQL API, the user calls it with a Tier 1 key. Each query is estimated first, drawn from the allowance and then the balance, and refused before it runs if they cannot cover it.

LAB PAYING BY INVOICE.
1. The PI signs in with GitHub, creates the team "Lab X", and enters the institution's name, billing contact and VAT or tax ID if it has one.
2. Requests a quote for a $500 prepaid block, enough for about 3.6 TiB of metered transfer at $0.135/GiB, and enters the PO number.
3. We issue an invoice through Paddle's manual collection (PO number, net-30 terms, bank transfer or card) or through Stripe Invoicing. When the PO arrives, the team wallet gets a provisional credit up to the PO amount, or credit on payment if the owner prefers.
4. The PI invites three members by GitHub login. Each signs in once and creates a key, which draws on the team wallet within a member cap the PI sets (for example $100/month).
5. Members work exactly as in the GPU-pod journey. Quotes show "Lab X wallet: $412.30".
6. The PI gets emails at 50%, 80% and 100% of the block. At zero, metered access stops for the team, Tier 0 keeps working, and no overage invoice is ever sent.
7. On the 1st, a statement CSV arrives listing member, object, bytes, cost and citations, for grant reporting. Unused credit carries over for 24 months, and the PI can ask for a refund at the end of the grant year.
design: friction.costModel:
PRICES USED:
- GCS internet egress: $0.12/GiB for 0–10 TiB; Standard storage about $0.02/GiB-month (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).
- Always Free: 100 GB/month of egress from North America and 5 GB-months of storage in us-east1 (https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features).
- Cloud Run request-based free tier: 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests a month (https://cloud.google.com/run/pricing).
- Identity Platform: social sign-in free to 50,000 MAU.
- Firestore: 50,000 reads and 20,000 writes a day free.
- BigQuery: first 10 GiB of storage free, about $0.023/GiB-month after that; 1 TiB/month of queries free for the querier.
- Merchant-of-record fees: about 10% on a $10 top-up and about 7–8% on $25.

NOW (assumptions: 50 full-release fetches a month at 0.2528 GiB each = 12.6 GiB; 1,000 Atlas visits at about 4 MB = 3.9 GiB; under 1 GB stored; no metered objects yet; few sign-ins):
- Our cost:
  - Egress: 16.5 GiB, inside the free 100 GB, so $0. Even fully billed it would be $1.98.
  - Storage: $0.
  - New components: $0. That covers Identity Platform, the Cloud Run broker, Firestore, BigQuery storage (under 10 GiB), the merchant of record (no monthly fee) and the HF mirror.
  - Allowance pool: about $0 in practice, capped at $50.
  - Total: about $0–2/month. Worst case is bounded at about $52.
- User's cost: $0 for everything published today, by every path.

100x (assumptions: 5,000 full fetches; 100,000 visits; 20 GiB of metered phase-2 or model objects; 200 paying users averaging 20 GiB/month; 5,000 signed-in MAU):
- Open tier, GCS only: 1,264 GiB + 381 GiB − 93 GiB free = 1,552 GiB, so about $186/month. That is inside the $200 budget, but a normal spike reaches the 150% ($300) kill switch and takes the data offline.
- Open tier, fetch_data.py reading the HF mirror first (10% falling back to GCS): 126 + 381 − 93 = 414 GiB, so about $50/month. Moving web data to a zero-egress host would take this to about $5.
- Metered, in the second project:
  - 4,000 GiB of egress costs $480.
  - Revenue: 4,000 × $0.135 = $540 gross.
  - Fees: $38–54.
  - Net: +$6 to +$22, 1–4% over cost, trued up by the quarterly reconciliation.
- Allowance pool: at most $50.
- Storage: metered bucket about $0.40, BigQuery about $0.23, Requester Pays copy $0 extra if it is the same bucket (about $0.40 if a second one).
- Identity Platform: 5,000 MAU, $0.
- Cloud Run: about 200,000 requests, $0.
- Firestore: $0.
- Total at 100x: about $100/month net with the mirror, about $240 without it.

USER'S COST AT 100x:
- Open: $0.
- Signed in: $0 for up to 7.4 GiB/month of metered data.
- A paying user taking 20 GiB/month: $2.70/month, so one $10 top-up lasts about 3.7 months.
- A lab: a $500 block covers about 3.6 TiB.
- BYO-cloud: 20 GiB × $0.12 = $2.40 to the internet, $0 into us-east1 compute.
- BigQuery: $0 within 1 TiB/month, then $6.25/TiB.

Takeaway: the free tier, not the paid one, is what threatens the budget at scale. The zero-egress mirror is what keeps both Tier 0 free and the $200 budget intact.
design: friction.terms:
How each source recorded in manifest 2026-10-18 interacts with charging:
- AFND: no_restriction_found (checked 2026-08-25; #117, policy #149). Chargeable. 113 objects. Carry the citation of Gonzalez-Galarza et al. 2020.
- MAP: no_restriction_found (checked 2026-10-18; the open-access policy asks users to cite the original sources). Chargeable. Carry the Piel 2013 and Howes 2012 citations.
- CPIC: CC0-1.0. Chargeable.
- ClinVar: no_restriction_found, and asks for attribution. Chargeable. Attribution travels with every object.
- GeneReviews: restriction_found and non_commercial = true. Never metered under R2. Its 6 objects (the curated registry tables and sources/curated, which hold links only) stay open. Any future object combining it with chargeable data is also unmeterable unless split.
- WorldPop: not_checked. 62 objects, every surface. Free only. Recording a terms check is the prerequisite for ever charging for surfaces or models.
- genomeos (project-authored): not_checked, because the README's Apache-2.0 covers code and docs only. 103 objects, free only. The owner must choose a data licence before any project output (exported fits, #471) can be metered. CC BY 4.0 is the choice that also qualifies for AWS Open Data sponsorship (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
- Phase 2:
  - gnomAD is explicitly_open (CC0) but its SpliceAI fields are CC BY-NC.
  - AlphaGenome is explicitly_open but its top_attributions field is non-commercial.
  - Both must ship their restricted fields as separate, free-only objects (or not at all), so that the permissive remainder can be metered if it ever exceeds 1 GiB. The existing KNOWN_NON_COMMERCIAL_FIELDS tripwire already forces those fields to be declared.
  - dbSNP: no_restriction_found, chargeable.
- All of Us: never served in any tier, paid or free (AGENTS.md).

Why we never charge for non-commercial data, even at cost:
- CC BY-NC 4.0 defines NonCommercial as \"not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation\" (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/legalcode.en). Pure cost recovery may pass that test, but only the licensor can say so.
- The merchant of record also makes us attest that \"you hold all necessary rights and licenses to distribute the product\" (https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/eligibility). We cannot attest that for not_checked sources.
- The rule therefore avoids the question rather than arguing it: CHARGEABLE is an allowlist.
- The only paid-adjacent route for non-commercial data is byo_cloud, by explicit override. There Google bills the user for its own transfer and we receive nothing.

Attribution survives every path:
- The quote, the receipt, the statement CSV, the BigQuery table descriptions, the HF dataset card and each Download panel all carry the manifest's sources block (name, citation, terms_url, status, note).
- The terms of service and every receipt say: \"You are paying for network transfer and compute at cost. No fee is charged for the data or for a licence. Each dataset remains under its source's terms; cite as listed.\"
- Identity: ORCID's Public API cannot gate a revenue-generating service (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/), so it is excluded until ORCID agrees.
build: 1. Policy doc and owner-decision issue (no code). docs/access-tiers.md sets out the tiers, the rule R1–R5 with its constants, the prices, the no-surprise rules and the journeys. A `needs-human-decision` issue lists the decisions: who the legal seller is, which merchant of record (Paddle or Stripe Managed Payments), a data licence for project-authored outputs, a WorldPop terms check, the size of the allowance pool, and whether team credit starts on PO or on payment.

2. Manifest schema v2 with `access`. Add `access` (open|metered|byo_cloud) and `served_from` to each object, plus an `access_policy` block holding the constants, in genomeos/publication/data_release.py. build_data_release.py computes access by R1–R5 and the release cap, with an ACCESS_OVERRIDES table. Every way the rule can fail gets a hard-error test. Rebuilding 2026-10-18 must give all 248 objects `open`. fetch_data.py reads v1 and v2. Module docstrings cite the spec section.

3. Zero-egress mirror. Commit MIRRORS (the existing public HF dataset, $0 egress) in data_release.py. Extend scripts/sync_store.py to push each release under its exact keys. Add `--source auto|gcs|hf` to fetch_data.py: auto reads HF first and falls back to GCS on a 403, a 5xx or a hash mismatch, with sha256 checks unchanged. Add a CI job that runs `--verify-remote --source hf`. Result: the free tier keeps working when the kill switch trips.

4. Browser SQL. Add Content-Range and Accept-Ranges to `responseHeader` in deploy/data-store-cors.json, and verify that a ranged GET returns 206. Recent DuckDB-WASM versions are reported to need Content-Range exposed (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-wasm/issues/1852). Add docs with DuckDB examples against the release keys. In a separate PR, add a 'Query in your browser' panel to the Atlas with a pinned DuckDB-WASM and httpfs, served from GCS rather than HF, because HF's cross-host redirect breaks CORS preflight (https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/issues/7931).

5. Single-file fetcher. A CI step builds fetch_data.pyz, a stdlib zipapp that vendors data_release.py and the newest manifest, and attaches it to each GitHub release, so `curl -LO …/fetch_data.pyz && python3 fetch_data.pyz` works without a clone.

6. BYO-cloud downloads. Add `--billing-project` to fetch_data.py with stdlib token sources: an env var filled from `gcloud auth print-access-token`, a refresh from the authorized_user ADC file, or the metadata server. It prints a list-price quote and enforces `--max-spend`. Add an owner-run provisioning script (dry-run first) for a Requester Pays bucket in a second project. Document a test of a signed URL with userProject against it. If that fails, the broker gets its own non-RP bucket.

7. BigQuery lane. A publish step loads each release's open (and later metered) Parquet into native tables in a dataset per release, `atlas_<release>`, co-located with the bucket so reads never cross regions. Table descriptions carry the citations and terms, and the dataset ACL gives allAuthenticatedUsers READER. Test that a fresh sandbox account can query it; that is not yet verified.

8. Broker core, with no money yet. services/access_broker/ is FastAPI on Cloud Run in project 2. Pure modules genomeos/access/{pricing,ledger,quota}.py have no HTTP and are unit-tested directly. Firebase ID-token verification. Hashed API keys. `/v1/quote` and `/v1/fetch` return 15-minute V4 signed URLs signed through IAM signBlob, with no stored key. Idempotent debits, the $1 allowance and the $50 pool, caps per key, and the re-issue policy.

9. CLI auth. `fetch_data.py login` (device flow against the broker's /device endpoints), support for GENOMEOS_API_KEY, the credential file at mode 0600, routing of metered objects through the broker, quotes, `--max-spend`, and an exit code of 3 for 'needs sign-in or credit'.

10. Website account page and download panel. Firebase sign-in with GitHub and Google; keys (create, name, cap, revoke); allowance and balance; history with citations; the price table. The download panel shows size, sha256, citation and the label 'free' or the price.

11. Payments, behind a flag until the decisions in step 1 are made. Merchant-of-record checkout top-ups of at least $10, a webhook that credits the ledger idempotently, receipts that state the terms, refunds, and no stored card by default.

12. Teams and invoices. Team wallets, invites by GitHub login or verified email, caps per member, quote to invoice (Paddle manual collection with PO and terms, or Stripe Invoicing), and statement CSVs.

13. Cost reconciliation. A monthly job joins the billing export with the ledger, publishes a cost-recovery report, and alerts when recovery falls outside 95–105%. Price changes go through a PR to pricing.py.

14. Hosted query metering, only if the parallel design ships a query service. Bounded endpoints stay anonymous with rate limits per IP. SQL endpoints need a key, are estimated first, and are debited at measured Cloud Run cost divided by 0.89.
risks: No seller exists yet. A merchant of record still needs a legal entity or a person to pass its eligibility review and receive payouts. Stripe Managed Payments supports US businesses but not one-off invoices, and excludes buyers in China (https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/eligibility). Owner decision. Until it is made, steps 11–12 stay behind a flag and the metered tier runs on allowances only.

Kill-switch coupling. If metered egress shares the free tier's project, paid downloads count against the $200 budget and can make the free bucket private for everyone. Mitigation: a second project. Its own budget only alerts, and the broker's prepaid-only issuance is its hard cap.

Free-tier growth. At 100x, GCS-only free egress reaches about $186/month and one spike trips the 150% switch. Mitigation: the HF mirror first. If HF throttles, its rate limit is 3,000 anonymous resolver requests per IP per 5 minutes (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/rate-limits). HF public storage is 'best-effort' (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-limits). Plan B is applying to AWS Open Data or Google Public Datasets for the open tier.

Leaked or reused signed URLs keep working until they expire, and signed URLs keep working after the kill switch fires. Mitigation: 15-minute expiry, a charge per URL issued, a cap on re-issues, and a separate metered bucket that the kill switch does not cover.

Terms mistakes. The vocabularies differ (restriction_found in the release, restricted in the web catalog). A source can also gain a new restricted field. CHARGEABLE is an allowlist, so an unknown status blocks metering. The tripwire only catches restrictions already known, so a new field still needs its own check (docs/non-commercial-data.md).

Not verified, so test first: whether a BigQuery sandbox can query a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset; whether a V4 signed URL against a Requester Pays bucket needs userProject in the signed request; DuckDB-WASM range reads against GCS with the CORS change; and whether DuckDB-WASM's HEAD probe fails on signed URLs that allow only GET (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-wasm/issues/1367), which would push metered browser SQL to the CLI.

Abuse of the free allowance with throwaway GitHub accounts. The $50 global pool bounds the loss. If it is drained repeatedly, require a GitHub account at least 30 days old, or the first top-up, before the allowance applies. Card testing on top-ups is handled by the merchant of record's fraud screening.

Ledger bugs could overcharge or undercharge. Mitigation: pure, unit-tested pricing and ledger modules, idempotency keys, an append-only ledger, and the monthly reconciliation against the billing export.

Liability for prepaid balances, and consumer law (cooling-off periods, refunds). The merchant of record applies regional cooling-off rules and can refund within 60 days (https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/eligibility). Our side: refunds on request and 24-month validity.

Privacy. Usage logs reveal which variants a researcher studies. Mitigation: minimal fields, 13-month retention, no third-party analytics, a privacy notice. This needs GDPR-grade handling for EU users.

Institution-managed Google accounts sometimes cannot create projects, which blocks the BigQuery sandbox and Requester Pays for those users. Tiers 1–3 avoid this, because GitHub sign-in needs no cloud project.

Operational load. Support email, refunds, disputes and quote requests are work for maintainers that costs no money. Mitigation: build the paid tier only when the first metered object exists. Today the rule puts everything in Tier 0.
whyNotOthers: Requester Pays as the first paid step. The user needs a Google account, a billing account with a card, a project and the Service Usage Consumer role (https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays). That is the 'cloud billing account' rung of the friction ladder. Kept as optional Lane C for users who already have it, never as the only route.

Postpaid usage billing (monthly metered invoices, for example Stripe Billing usage pricing at 0.7% of volume, https://stripe.com/billing/pricing). It produces exactly the surprise bills the angle forbids, and bad debt on a $200 budget. Prepaid only.

Subscriptions or flat plans, including a Cloud Marketplace data product. A commitment before any exploration, and not 'just enough to recoup'. Marketplace also needs Partner Network membership and a 3% fee, and supports flat subscriptions, not metering (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-cloud-marketplace).

A login wall on all data (HF gated datasets, GBIF-style accounts for bulk downloads). It breaks anonymous fetch_data.py and the owner's promise that today's datasets are free to distribute. It also rules out AWS Open Data, which does not allow gated access (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/).
Charging each download directly by card. Stripe's 30¢ fixed fee is ten times the $0.03 cost of a full release (https://stripe.com/pricing). Prepaid balances spread the fee across many downloads.

Apigee monetization. Environments start at $365/month, over the whole budget. Monetization comes only with a Subscription, and payment collection still falls to us (https://cloud.google.com/apigee/pricing, https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/monetization/overview).

API Gateway or Endpoints quotas. Every consumer needs their own GCP project and API key, which is more friction than our own keys, and nobody gets billed (https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/quotas-overview).

Credits or token units in place of dollars. They hide the price, and OpenAlex moved from credit units to dollars (https://help.openalex.org/access/pricing/). Showing dollars at list price plus fees is the most honest way to say 'just enough to recoup'.

ORCID as the sign-in. Its Public API terms forbid use in connection with a revenue-generating service, and it returns no email (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/). GitHub and Google cover researchers at no cost.

Earth Engine-style 'add a card to unlock more free quota' (https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/noncommercial_tiers). It puts a card step in front of free use. Our free tier is generous enough without it, and the allowance pool limits abuse instead.

Cloud CDN in front of the free bucket now. Forwarding rules cost about $18/month fixed and it pays back only above roughly 500 GiB/month (https://cloud.google.com/cdn/pricing). The HF mirror cuts egress to about $0 with no fixed cost.

Our own Stripe account plus Stripe Tax, without a merchant of record. Cheaper (2.9% + 30¢ plus 0.5%), but we would have to register for EU VAT from the first sale to an EU consumer (https://vat-one-stop-shop.ec.europa.eu/one-stop-shop_en), and handle sales tax and disputes ourselves. Worth revisiting only if volume makes the roughly 3.5–5% merchant-of-record premium matter.

design: recovery.title: genomeOS Atlas access tiers: Google bills heavy users directly, so we run no login or billing ourselves
design: recovery.summary:
Recommendation for the least-to-build, least-to-run angle. Three doors, and genomeOS runs no login, billing, ledger or query server for any of them. Google accounts are the login and Google Cloud Billing is the biller.

(0) OPEN. Everything published today stays anonymous and free on the public bucket (genomeos-atlas-data) and the Atlas site. scripts/fetch_data.py stays standard-library only.

(1) SQL. The same tables, loaded as native BigQuery tables and shared with allAuthenticatedUsers. Anyone signed in to Google queries from their own project, and BigQuery bills that project, not ours. That costs them nothing within 1 TiB a month, and the sandbox needs no card.

(2) BULK. A separate Requester Pays bucket for the future heavy objects: phase-2 raw harvests (#472), safe-exported models (#471) and large derived products. Google bills each requester's own billing account at list price, with no markup. That is exactly "just enough to recoup", and we never touch money.

A mechanical rule in build_data_release.py writes a `tier` field for every object in the manifest. The rule is first match wins: reused keys keep their tier; anything non-commercial or restricted is open; today's dataset classes are open; objects of 64 MiB or less are open; everything else is requester_pays, but only if every source has a positive terms finding. A release guard caps the open tier at 1 GiB per release, so the worst-case cost of a free full download stays at $0.12 or less.

Our bill is storage, about $0-3 a month even at 100x, plus anonymous open-tier egress. Egress is the only variable line, and the existing kill switch bounds it. The build is about 5 PR-sized steps: two are repo-only, two need an owner to provision a bucket or dataset, and one is client code.

Explicitly deferred behind triggers: a card-payment broker for people without a cloud account (Stripe plus signed URLs), and sponsor mirrors (Google Public Datasets, AWS ODP).

I re-checked the pricing and feature claims against the live Google, Hugging Face and licence pages on 2026-10-18. Claims marked "(scout)" come from the parallel research pass on the same day. No cloud commands were run and no repo files were written.
design: recovery.tiers:
TIER 0 - OPEN (anonymous, free, for good).
- What: every object the rule marks `open`. Today that is all 248 objects in release 2026-10-18 (271,494,507 bytes, about 0.25 GiB): registries, sources, raw/afnd_populations.tsv, store/artifacts (surface cells.parquet plus manifest.json, at most 7.5 MB each), validation evidence, the catalog and inventory, and the manifests. Observation tables join this class when they are published. Any later object of 64 MiB or less is also open.
- Who: anyone, with no account.
- How: plain HTTPS GET of https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/<key>, using the keys in the committed manifest. Or `python scripts/fetch_data.py` (stdlib, sha256-checked), or DuckDB range reads of the Parquet, which fetch only the columns a query needs (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/httpfs/https.html), or the Atlas site (the genomeos-atlas-web bucket).
- Cost to them: $0.
- Cost to us: internet egress at $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB a month, after 100 GB a month of Always Free egress from North America (us-east1 qualifies). A full release costs about $0.03 and one surface about $0.001 (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).

TIER 1 - SQL (Google sign-in, free to nearly everyone).
- What: the Tier 0 tables as native BigQuery tables in the US multi-region. US multi-region is where bigquery-public-data, including gnomAD, lives, and a table in another region can't be joined with them (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data). They sit in a dedicated public project, with one dataset per immutable release plus `latest` views. Dataset access is READER for the specialGroup allAuthenticatedUsers (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/control-access-to-resources-iam). A free BigQuery sharing listing can be added for discovery; it has no cost for exchanges or listings (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analytics-hub-introduction).
- Who: anyone with a Google account. That can be any email address; Gmail isn't required (https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/27441).
- How: the BigQuery console, the bq CLI or client libraries, run from the user's own project. A sandbox project works with "no credit card or billing account" and gets 1 TiB of queries a month (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox).
- Cost to them: $0 within 1 TiB processed a month, then $6.25/TiB, with a minimum of 10 MB per table referenced (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).
- Cost to us: storage only. The first 10 GiB is free; above that, active storage is about $0.023/GiB-month and long-term $0.016. Batch loads are free. Per the pricing page: "The data owner is not charged when their data is accessed."

TIER 2 - BULK (Google sign-in plus the user's own billing project, at cost).
- What: objects the rule marks `requester_pays`: the phase-2 raw harvests, safe-exported fits, and large derived products. None exist yet.
- Who: anyone with a role holding serviceusage.services.use on a project with billing enabled. That can be their own project, or a role their PI grants them on the lab's project.
- How: a new bucket (proposed name genomeos-atlas-bulk; us-east1; Standard, or Coldline for cold classes) with Requester Pays on. Users run `fetch_data.py --billing-project P`, or `gcloud storage cp --billing-project=P`. Raw HTTP works too, with the header x-goog-user-project or the query parameter userProject (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/using-requester-pays). The requester pays "data processing and network usage", and storage "always" stays with the bucket's project. Requests with no billing project fail with 400 UserProjectMissing (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).
- Cost to them (Google list price): $0.12/GiB to the internet, $0.02/GiB to another North American region, and $0 for data transfer within us-east1. Plus Class B reads at $0.0004 per 1,000, and on Coldline a retrieval fee of $0.02/GiB (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).
- Cost to us: storage at $0.020/GiB-month Standard, or $0.004 Coldline.

NOT OFFERED (deferred): paying by card without a cloud account. See whyNotOthers and the trigger in the build steps.

OPTIONAL FREE MIRROR: the existing interim Hugging Face dataset (scripts/sync_store.py). Hugging Face pays its egress. Its free public storage is "Best-effort", and HF asks that large uploads be "as useful to the community as possible" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-limits).
design: recovery.freeLine:
Rule applied by build_data_release.py to every object, written to a new manifest field `tier` (`open` | `requester_pays`). It is evaluated in order, and the first match wins. The rule never decides WHETHER something is published: INCLUDE and the terms register still decide that. It only decides which door a published object goes through.

R0. Pickles and object-dtype .npy files are refused, as today.

R1. Reused key: an object whose bytes reuse a key from an earlier release keeps that release's tier. Once free, always free, because an immutable public copy can't be withdrawn.

R2. Terms gate: if any of the object's sources has `non_commercial: true`, or terms status `restricted` or `restriction_found` (the release manifest uses `restriction_found` for GeneReviews, while commercial_use.py uses `restricted`, so the rule treats both alike), the object is `open`. Restricted or non-commercial content never goes behind a door that someone pays to open.

R3. Class: if the path starts with an OPEN_CLASSES prefix, the object is `open`. OPEN_CLASSES is exactly today's published roots: registry/, sources/, raw/afnd_populations.tsv, store/artifacts/, store/INVENTORY.json, store/catalog-metadata.json, validation/, and manifests. The observation tables are added when they publish. This is the owner's "current datasets are fine to distribute this way".

R4. Size: if bytes <= SMALL_OBJECT_BYTES = 64 MiB, the object is `open`. One download costs us at most $0.0075, and Requester Pays friction would be out of proportion. The largest object today is 7.5 MB.

R5. Otherwise the object is `requester_pays`. That is allowed only if its path matches a BULK_CLASSES prefix (raw/ beyond the reviewed table, models/, bulk/) AND every source's status is in {explicitly_open, permission_granted, no_restriction_found}. A source with status `not_checked`, or any status outside the vocabulary, is a hard error. The fix is to record the terms check, or to split or shrink the object. It is never to guess a status.

R6. A path that matches no class rule is a hard error, the same as the existing "no reviewed source rule" error.

RELEASE GUARD: the sum of `open` bytes in a release must be <= OPEN_RELEASE_MAX_BYTES = 1 GiB (today about 0.25 GiB). Exceeding it is a hard error. Only an owner PR that raises the constant resolves it, and that PR states the new worst-case cost of one full free download (cap x $0.12/GiB) and whether a sponsor mirror is in place.

OPERATIONS:
- An anonymous GET of an `open` object is free to the reader, and we pay its egress.
- All hosted SQL runs in BigQuery and is billed to the querier's project (free up to 1 TiB a month).
- A GET of a `requester_pays` object is billed to the requester's billing project.
- genomeOS runs no server-side query engine whose compute it would pay for.

The constants live in a pure module (genomeos/publication/access_tiers.py, no HTTP). CI recomputes the tiers of every committed manifest and fails on any difference.
design: recovery.identity:
