genomeOS runs no identity system. There are no accounts, passwords, API keys, OAuth apps, user table or ORCID or GitHub client. Google IAM does the whole job.

- Tier 0 needs no identity at all.
- Tier 1 accepts any Google identity through the allAuthenticatedUsers dataset grant. That can be a personal account, a Workspace account, or a Google account created with any email address (https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/27441).
- Tier 2 accepts any Google identity that holds serviceusage.services.use on the billing project it names (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays). The bucket grants roles/storage.legacyObjectReader to allAuthenticatedUsers: read by key, no listing, the same model as the open bucket. Requests without a billing project fail regardless.

So the owner's "login credentials" is a Google sign-in. It is already the first step of every BigQuery or Cloud Storage tool, so it adds no new step for users.

fetch_data.py stays standard-library only and gets a token in one of three ways:
(a) the GENOMEOS_GCS_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable, filled from `gcloud auth print-access-token`, which lasts about an hour;
(b) the authorized_user ADC file written by `gcloud auth application-default login` (including `--no-launch-browser` on a headless pod), refreshed by POSTing its refresh_token to https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token with urllib (https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials, https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/native-app);
(c) the GCE or Cloud Run metadata server.
Tokens are never logged or written anywhere.

Privacy cost: BigQuery Data Access audit logs "can't be disabled" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/configure-data-access). Queriers' principals are therefore recorded in the public project's _Default log bucket, which keeps logs for 30 days by default, configurable down to 1 day (https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/quotas). Set a short retention or an exclusion filter, and say so on the data-access page.

ORCID is deliberately not used. Its Public API "may not" be used "in connection with any revenue-generating product or service" (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/) (scout). Using it would also require running Identity Platform and a broker.
design: recovery.billing:
Google Cloud Billing does all of it, on the user's own billing account.

- BigQuery: "You are charged for queries run against shared data. The data owner is not charged when their data is accessed" (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).
- Requester Pays: the requester's billing project pays data processing (operations and retrieval) and network charges (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays).

What genomeOS doesn't have to do: set prices, hold money, issue invoices or receipts, register for sales tax or VAT, keep a ledger, handle refunds, or chase bad debt. "Just enough to recoup" becomes exactly Google's list price with zero markup. Card-fee arithmetic never comes up; under Stripe a ~$0.03 recovery would be uncollectable against a 30-cent fixed fee (https://stripe.com/pricing) (scout).

What isn't recouped:
(1) Our storage, about $0-3 a month even at 100x.
(2) Tier 0 anonymous egress. That is the deliberate free tier, bounded by the 1 GiB open cap and by the existing kill switch at 150% of the $200 budget (docs/cost-controls.md).

Heavy users and CI can also choose to pay their own way on the FREE bucket. Buckets with Requester Pays disabled "still accept requests that include a billing project", and "charges are applied to the billing project supplied in the request" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/using-requester-pays). So `fetch_data.py --billing-project` works on both buckets.

Proposed switch mode (owner decision): at 150%, the kill switch turns Requester Pays ON for genomeos-atlas-data instead of removing allUsers. Anonymous reads then pause with 400 UserProjectMissing, while anyone with a billing project can carry on and pay their own way. This needs storage.buckets.update, and publish_data_store.py has to pass our billing project while the switch is on.

Institutions pay Google the way they already do: by PO or invoice through Internet2 NET+ resellers, or through Google invoiced billing (registered as a business for at least 1 year, expecting at least $40,000 a year of spend, payment by check or wire) (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/invoiced-billing).
userJourneys: FIRST-TIME VISITOR. (1) Opens the Atlas site, which is served from the public web bucket with no login. (2) Explores the map. (3) Opens 'Get the data', which says in one line: 'Everything here is free, with no account.' It shows the three doors and the citation block taken from the release manifest's `sources`. (4) Gets one surface in one of three ways. A plain link https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<release>/store/artifacts/<artifact>/cells.parquet (about 7.5 MB). A copyable DuckDB line, SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('<that URL>'), which range-reads only the columns it needs. Or, for the whole release, `git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/genomeOS/genomeOS && python scripts/fetch_data.py`, which downloads 0.27 GB and checks every sha256. (5) fetch_data.py prints the citations to use. Cost to them: $0. Cost to us: about $0.001 per surface and about $0.03 per full release (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing), or $0 while total egress stays inside the 100 GB/month Always Free allowance.

RESEARCHER ON A GPU POD WITHOUT A CLOUD ACCOUNT. (1) On the pod: `git clone --filter=blob:none ... && python scripts/fetch_data.py`. This is stdlib only and anonymous, and it covers every object published today, so most researchers stop here. (2) Later they want a bulk object, such as a raw harvest or an exported model. fetch_data.py skips requester_pays objects by default and prints the count, the GiB, and an estimate: 'about $3.00 to this machine at $0.12/GiB, billed by Google to your project; rerun with --billing-project'. If the owner keeps the Hugging Face mirror for that class, it prints the free `hf download` alternative too. (3) Getting a billing project: the easiest route is for the PI to grant Service Usage Consumer on the lab's project, so the researcher needs no card. Otherwise they create a Google account with any email, create a project and attach billing. That needs a card, and new accounts get a $300 credit for 90 days (https://docs.cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features; whether the trial credit covers Requester Pays egress is expected but not verified). (4) A token without installing anything on the pod: run `gcloud auth print-access-token` on a laptop, then `export GENOMEOS_GCS_ACCESS_TOKEN=...` on the pod; it lasts about an hour. For long jobs, install gcloud on the pod and run `gcloud auth application-default login --no-launch-browser`; fetch_data.py refreshes from that file with urllib. (5) `python scripts/fetch_data.py --prefix raw/ --billing-project LAB_PROJECT --yes` sends Authorization plus x-goog-user-project and verifies every sha256. Cost: 25 GiB x $0.12 = $3.00 on the lab's bill or the trial credit. It is $0 transfer if the job runs on GCE in us-east1. Cost to us: $0.

HEAVY SQL USER. (1) Explores with DuckDB over the open Parquet, or downloads the release once (about $0.03 to us) and queries it locally. Repeated full scans over HTTP are discouraged on the access page, because they put egress on our bill. (2) For scans across variants and joins with gnomAD or 1000 Genomes in bigquery-public-data, opens the BigQuery console, signs in with Google and creates a sandbox project with no card. Managed academic accounts 'must select an organization' (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox). (3) Queries `<public-project>.genomeos_atlas_<release>.<table>` or the `latest` views. A dry run shows the bytes, and the tables are clustered by variant and H3 parent so filtered queries scan megabytes. (4) The 1 TiB a month free covers about 100,000 minimum-size queries, at the 10 MB minimum per table. Beyond that they enable billing and pay $6.25/TiB to Google (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing). (5) Optionally they subscribe to the BigQuery sharing listing, which creates a linked dataset in their own project. Cost to them: $0 typically; $25 a month for a user who scans 5 TiB. Cost to us: $0 compute, and storage inside the 10 GiB free tier.

LAB PAYING BY INVOICE. (1) The PI asks university research computing for a Google Cloud project. Most US research universities buy Google Cloud through Internet2 NET+ resellers such as Carahsoft on a PO. An institution can also use Google invoiced billing if it qualifies (a business for at least 1 year, at least $40,000 a year of expected spend, payment by check or wire; https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/invoiced-billing). (2) IT creates a dedicated project, for example 'genomeos-access', under that billing account, so the genomeOS charges can be identified on the invoice. It grants lab members Service Usage Consumer for the bulk tier and BigQuery Job User for SQL. (3) Members pass `--billing-project` to fetch_data.py or `gcloud storage cp`, and run BigQuery jobs in that project. (4) The charges appear on the institution's monthly Google invoice. (5) Institutions on Internet2 NET+ or a reseller can have internet data transfer fees waived, up to 15% of their total monthly Google Cloud fees. The waiver isn't available to pay-as-you-go card customers (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/data-transfer-waiver). In practice, the bulk tier is often free for such a lab. (6) If procurement wants a quote, `fetch_data.py --estimate --prefix ...` prints the bytes and the list-price cost. genomeOS never issues an invoice, takes a PO or holds money. Cost to us: $0.
design: recovery.costModel:
ASSUMPTIONS. The data store has no analytics yet, so traffic is assumed. Today: 10 full-release downloads, 500 single-surface reads (7.5 MB each) and 20 CI --verify-remote runs a month, about 11 GiB. 100x: 1,000 full downloads and 50,000 surface reads, with CI unchanged.

PRICES:
- GCS (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing): internet egress $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB, after 100 GB/month Always Free from us-east1/us-central1/us-west1. Standard storage $0.000027397/GiB-hour (about $0.020/GiB-month). Coldline about $0.004/GiB-month, plus a retrieval fee of $0.02/GiB that the requester pays on a Requester Pays bucket. Class B reads $0.0004 per 1,000. Same-location transfer free. For transfer to BigQuery, GCS counts BigQuery US as us-central1.
- BigQuery (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing): 1 TiB/month of queries free, then $6.25/TiB. 10 GiB of storage free, then $0.023 active or $0.016 long-term per GiB-month. Batch loads free. Loading from a bucket in another location incurs data transfer charges (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/batch-loading-data), about $0.02/GiB.

NOW
- Us: open egress of 11 GiB sits inside the free 100 GB, so $0. About 0.5 GB of storage sits inside the 5 GB-month free tier, so $0. BigQuery is about 1 GiB, so $0. The per-release load costs about 0.25 GiB x $0.02, about $0.005. The bulk bucket is empty, so $0. The kill switch is about $0. Total: about $0-1 a month, flat.
- Users: $0 on every door. Even a billed full release would be only $0.03.

100x USERS, TODAY'S DATA
- Us: 607 GiB of open egress, so (607 - 93 free) x $0.12, about $62 a month. Everything else stays about $0.
- Users: $0.

100x USERS AND 100x DATA
Here the open tier is at its 1 GiB cap, the bulk tier adds 25 GiB per release with 100 GiB stored, and BigQuery holds 50 GiB.
- Us:
  - Open egress of 1,369 GiB: about $153 a month. This is the only line that grows with usage.
  - Bulk storage: $2.00 on Standard, or $0.40 on Coldline.
  - BigQuery storage: $0.64-0.92.
  - Loads: about $0.02 per release.
  - Total: about $155 a month. That is under $200 but past the 50% email threshold, which is the agreed trigger to apply to Google Public Datasets (bq-public-data@google.com; https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data) or AWS ODP. ODP covers 'storage ... as well as distribution costs such as egress' (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/) (scout). Once open egress moves to a sponsor, our total is about $3 a month, flat.
- Users:
  - Bulk, 25 GiB to an internet pod: $3.00, plus $0.50 if stored on Coldline.
  - Bulk to GCE in us-east1: $0 transfer.
  - Bulk to another North American region: $0.50.
  - BigQuery, typical user: $0.
  - BigQuery, a user scanning 5 TiB a month: $25.
  - A lab on an Internet2 NET+ or reseller account: internet egress is waived up to 15% of its total monthly Google Cloud fees.

WORST CASE (abuse)
- A scripted loop on the open bucket is limited only by the kill switch, which acts at $300 of actual spend, hours late because billing data lags.
- Abuse of the bulk bucket or BigQuery costs us $0, because the abuser's own project is billed.
- The web bucket's egress is NOT covered by the switch.
design: recovery.terms:
Charging in this design: genomeOS collects no money on any door. In Tiers 1-2, Google bills its own customer for compute and transport under that customer's agreement with Google. Creative Commons defines NonCommercial as 'not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation' (https://wiki.creativecommons.org/wiki/NonCommercial_interpretation), and nothing in this design compensates genomeOS. The rule still keeps non-commercial and restricted content open-only (R2), so the design never depends on that argument.

Per source, as recorded in data/releases/2026-10-18.json:
- afnd: no_restriction_found (checked 2026-08-25; policy #149; non_commercial false). Any tier. Carry the Gonzalez-Galarza et al. citation. Keep the AFND HTML page caches out of every release (INCLUDE): they are a cache of AFND's web pages, not data.
- map: no_restriction_found (checked 2026-10-18). MAP's policy says 'There are no restrictions to access or use of the data' and asks that 'the original source details ... are cited' (https://malariaatlas.org/open-access-policy/). Any tier, with the citations carried.
- cpic: CC0-1.0. Any tier.
- clinvar: no_restriction_found. It 'asks downstream users to attribute'. Any tier, with attribution.
- genereviews: restriction_found plus non_commercial true. R2 makes it open-only, so it never reaches a paid door. Today it is links and identifiers only, not chapter content.
- worldpop: not_checked. It may be open, which covers today's surfaces. It blocks requester_pays (R5) until a check is recorded. WorldPop's hub footer states CC BY 4.0 (https://hub.worldpop.org/), so a recorded check would probably allow any tier with attribution. That is for a PR to record; the builder must not assume it.
- genomeos (project-authored): not_checked, with no data licence recorded (design spec §9.3). Exported models (#471) and project-authored bulk products cannot go requester_pays until the owner picks a data licence, for example CC BY 4.0 or CC0.

Field-level restrictions: KNOWN_NON_COMMERCIAL_FIELDS (gnomad.spliceai, alphagenome.top_attributions) appear in no release payload today. If they ever do, they are open-only. If that would break the 1 GiB guard, the build fails, and the fix is the field-level extraction commercial_use.py already supports, or written permission.

Attribution on every door:
- the manifest's `sources` block sits next to the data in both buckets;
- each BigQuery release dataset gets a `sources` table, plus dataset and table descriptions with the citation and terms_url;
- column descriptions name any restricted field;
- fetch_data.py prints the citations.

Mirrors: AWS ODP refuses non-commercial licences and gated access (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/) (scout), so any ODP or Public Datasets mirror must leave out GeneReviews-sourced objects. ORCID isn't used, so its no-revenue clause never applies. If a card-payment tier is ever built, R2 must extend to 'never sold', and ORCID must not gate it.
build: PR 1. Tier rule and manifest v2. Repo only, no cloud. (a) Add genomeos/publication/access_tiers.py: a pure function with no HTTP, holding OPEN_CLASSES, BULK_CLASSES, SMALL_OBJECT_BYTES=64 MiB, OPEN_RELEASE_MAX_BYTES=1 GiB, and the POSITIVE and RESTRICTED status sets, including `restriction_found`. It cites the design section. (b) build_data_release.py writes a per-object `tier` and enforces R1-R6 and the release guard as hard errors. (c) data_release.validate_manifest accepts schema v1 (implicitly all open) and v2. (d) CI recomputes the tiers of every committed manifest. (e) Unit tests for each branch: non-commercial goes open; not_checked, bulk and large is an error; a reused key keeps its tier; the guard fails above the cap; an unclaimed path is an error. Today's releases come out entirely open, so behaviour doesn't change.

PR 2. docs/data-access.md and a 'Get the data' section on the website. Repo only. It covers the three doors, the free line in plain words, worked costs ($0.03 per release; $0.12/GiB for bulk; 1 TiB of BigQuery free), the citation block, and links to Google research credits, Internet2 NET+ and the data transfer waiver. It also covers the audit-log privacy notice and when the kill switch fires. Update docs/data-store.md §9.2 so it records Requester Pays as a separate bucket, never the open one.

PR 3. fetch_data.py becomes tier-aware, still standard-library only. By default it skips requester_pays objects and prints an estimate. New: `--billing-project`; tokens from GENOMEOS_GCS_ACCESS_TOKEN, an authorized_user ADC refresh through urllib, or the metadata server; Authorization plus x-goog-user-project headers; `--estimate`; and `--yes`, required when the estimate is over $1. A 400 UserProjectMissing response gets a plain explanation. The same flag lets anyone pay their own way on the open bucket. Tests run against the loopback fake server: no token is ever printed, and a bulk URL that isn't the committed one is refused.

PR 4. The bulk bucket. The owner runs it once, and it ships when the first requester_pays object exists (#471 or #472). Add scripts/provision_bulk_bucket.py, idempotent with --dry-run, in the style of provision_data_store_bucket.py. It creates genomeos-atlas-bulk in us-east1: uniform access, Requester Pays on, roles/storage.legacyObjectReader for allAuthenticatedUsers (no listing), versioning and soft delete, and Standard or Coldline per class. It grants data-store-publisher objectCreator plus dataStoreReader on the bucket and Service Usage Consumer on our project. Commit the DATA_STORE_BULK_BUCKET and URL constants. publish_data_store.py routes each object by tier and passes our billing project for bulk uploads. The bucket needs no kill switch, because its egress isn't ours.

PR 5. BigQuery publishing. Owner decision first: a dedicated public project whose id may be committed, with docs/repo-gcloud-auth.md amended, because a shared table's path exposes the project id. Then scripts/provision_bigquery_public.py and scripts/publish_bigquery.py: one dataset per release in the US multi-region; native tables (not external) loaded from the open bucket with WRITE_EMPTY; partitioning and clustering as the parallel storage/query design defines; a `sources` table and descriptions; `latest` views; READER for allAuthenticatedUsers; a short retention or an exclusion filter for the Data Access logs; the new project added to the $200 budget's scope. A smoke test from a separate sandbox project verifies that sandbox queries of a third party's shared dataset work, which is the main untested assumption.
PR 6 (optional). A BigQuery sharing listing in a public exchange, at no cost. It gives discovery and per-organization usage metrics without running a login.

PR 7 (optional, owner decision #480 follow-up). Kill-switch 'pay-your-own-way' mode: at 150% it sets requesterPays on genomeos-atlas-data instead of removing allUsers. The custom role swaps setIamPolicy for storage.buckets.update. The docs and the fetch_data.py message point to --billing-project.

TRIGGERS (do nothing until one fires). (a) Open egress above $50 a month for two months, or a PR that raises OPEN_RELEASE_MAX_BYTES: apply to Google Public Datasets (bq-public-data@google.com) and AWS ODP for the open tier, excluding non-commercial objects. (b) Five or more documented users in a quarter who need a bulk object and cannot use Google Cloud billing: first offer the Hugging Face mirror for that class. Only after that, design a card-payment broker.
risks: The bulk tier excludes some people. A Google Cloud billing account needs a card, even for the $300 trial (https://docs.cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features). Managed academic accounts 'must select an organization' and may be unable to create projects (https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/sandbox). Some countries and institutions can't use Google Cloud at all. Mitigations: R4 keeps most objects free; a PI can grant a role on the lab's project; Google research credits for faculty, PhD students and postdocs at eligible institutions, expiring 365 days after redemption (https://edu.google.com/programs/credits/research/); the Internet2 NET+ data transfer waiver; the optional Hugging Face mirror; and the trigger for a card-payment broker.

Tier 0 egress has no limit per user. One scripted loop can trip the kill switch, and that takes the open bucket offline for everyone, hours late because billing data lags. The 1 GiB open cap bounds what each download costs; it doesn't limit how many downloads happen. PR 7's switch mode and a sponsor mirror reduce the damage.

'Flat' is not guaranteed at 100x. The open tier alone is estimated at $60-155 a month, which crosses the 50% budget email. The bill stays flat only if a sponsor mirror lands or the cap stays tight. Acceptance into Google Public Datasets and AWS ODP is discretionary, with no published criteria and no SLA.
The Atlas web bucket's egress is outside the kill switch and outside these tiers (docs/cost-controls.md). It needs its own estimate, and it could become the bigger line.
BigQuery sharing exposes a project id, which the current repo rule forbids committing. This needs a dedicated public project and an owner amendment to docs/repo-gcloud-auth.md.

Domain-restricted sharing: an organization created on or after 2024-05-03 enforces iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains by default. That blocks allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers unless a tag-based exception is set up (https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/restricting-domains). If the project ever moves under such an organization, the open bucket, the bulk bucket and the BigQuery sharing would all stop working.

Personal data: BigQuery Data Access audit logs 'can't be disabled' (https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/configure-data-access), so queriers' principals end up in our logs. Set a short retention or an exclusion filter, and disclose it.

Not verified, and each has a test step: whether a sandbox project can query a third party's allAuthenticatedUsers dataset or subscribe to a sharing listing; whether DuckDB EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS with x-goog-user-project can read a Requester Pays bucket; whether trial credits cover Requester Pays egress; the exact transfer charge for loading data across locations.

Requesters can get surprise bills. Egress costs $0.23/GiB to China and $0.19/GiB to Australia (https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing), and GCS has no per-bucket line item on the requester's invoice. Mitigations: fetch_data.py prints an estimate and asks for confirmation, and the docs recommend a dedicated project.
Immutability makes misclassification permanent. An object published open stays free forever (R1). Tiers must be reviewed in the release PR before the first upload.

Storage is never recouped. At TB scale, bulk storage on Standard ($20 per TB-month) would erode the $200 budget. Use Coldline for cold classes, where the requester pays retrieval (watch the 90-day minimum storage duration; it doesn't matter here because nothing is deleted), and pursue sponsors.
PR 7's switch mode needs storage.buckets.update, which is as powerful as today's setIamPolicy. It is the owner's call.
If the owner keeps the Hugging Face mirror for bulk classes, the bulk tier sees little use. That is fine for cost, but it depends on HF's 'Best-effort' free public storage policy.

The status vocabulary is split. The release manifest uses `restriction_found` and commercial_use.py uses `restricted`. The rule must treat both as restricted and fail on unknown statuses, or a restriction could slip into the bulk tier.
whyNotOthers: Our own login, metering and Stripe or Paddle top-ups behind a Cloud Run signed-URL broker. This is the only way to bill people without a cloud account. But we would own authentication, a ledger, pricing, receipts, refunds, VAT and sales tax, a merchant entity, support and abuse handling. Card fees are 2.9% plus 30 cents, so a $10 top-up loses $0.59 and the ~$0.03 per-release cost can't be charged at all (https://stripe.com/pricing) (scout). Signed URLs keep working after the kill switch fires, so the broker would need its own spend cap. Collecting money is also exactly where non-commercial terms and ORCID's no-revenue clause bite (https://info.orcid.org/public-client-terms-of-service/). Deferred behind a demand trigger.

Requester Pays on the existing open bucket. It ends anonymous reads with 400 UserProjectMissing (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/requester-pays), breaking fetch_data.py, every clone, and the owner's 'current datasets free' requirement. It is acceptable only as the emergency switch mode in PR 7.

A hosted DuckDB, Postgres or API query server on Cloud Run. It puts query compute and abuse on our bill and needs our own authentication and metering. BigQuery with allAuthenticatedUsers sharing gives querier-pays for free: 'The data owner is not charged' (https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing).

OpenAlex-style API keys with daily dollar allowances. Good user experience, but it is a metered service we would have to run (key issuance, ledger, rate limiter). It is only worth it once we run a hosted API whose compute we pay for, and this design deliberately has none (https://help.openalex.org/api-reference/authentication) (scout).

Selling through a Cloud Marketplace data product. It needs Partner Network membership and 'enterprise-ready' operations, a PADFA attestation (genetic information is listed), and a 3% fee, and it offers flat subscriptions, not metering (https://cloud.google.com/terms/marketplace-revenue-share-schedule, https://docs.cloud.google.com/marketplace/docs/partners/data) (scout).

Apigee monetization. Pay-as-you-go environments start at $365 a month, more than the whole budget; monetization is for subscription organizations only; and it still needs a payment processor (https://cloud.google.com/apigee/pricing) (scout).

API Gateway or Cloud Endpoints quotas. They count and throttle calls but bill nobody, and every consumer needs their own Google Cloud project and an API key (https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/quotas-overview) (scout).

Cloud CDN in front of the open bucket. It cuts egress to $0.08/GiB but adds a fixed forwarding-rule cost of about $18 a month and recovers nothing. By the scout's arithmetic it pays for itself only above about 500 GiB a month (https://cloud.google.com/cdn/pricing) (scout). Revisit only if no sponsor accepts us.

Sponsor programs (Google Public Datasets, AWS ODP) as the whole design. They make Tier 0 free to us, but they can't host a login or paid tier. ODP requires open licences and no gating, and acceptance is discretionary (https://aws.amazon.com/opendata/faqs/) (scout). So they are the scale-up trigger for Tier 0, not the access layer.

Invoicing labs ourselves (quotes, POs, Stripe Invoicing). That is a sales motion, a merchant entity and tax work. Universities already pay Google by PO through NET+ resellers or Google invoiced billing, so the invoice already exists on Google's side (https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/invoiced-billing).
Hugging Face gated datasets as the paid tier. Gating is a login wall, not billing (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/datasets-gated) (scout). It works as a free mirror, not as cost recovery.

judge + synthesise.recommendation:
I recommend Design B ("Google bills heavy users directly") as the base, with the best parts of A and C added. Everything published today stays free and anonymous, and the release builder enforces that. An object is free if it is one of today's kinds of data, if one download costs us 12 cents or less (1 GiB or smaller), or if a free mirror carries it. Only larger objects are "at cost". Data whose terms are restricted, non-commercial or unchecked never goes behind any payment.

At first, the paid door is Google's: a separate Requester Pays bucket and a public BigQuery dataset in the US multi-region. The login is the user's Google account, and Google bills the user's own or their lab's account at list price. We hold no money, accounts or invoices, so "just enough to recoup" holds by construction.

From C: fetch_data.py tries a free mirror first, with sponsor programs as the step for later growth, because the free tier's popularity is what actually threatens the $200 budget. That is about $186 a month at 100x traffic from GCS alone, versus about $49 with the mirror.

From A: the prepaid card door (GitHub or Google sign-in, device-code login on pods, $10 top-ups through a merchant of record, quote before every charge, no bills afterwards) is fully specified as Phase 3. It gets built when the first at-cost object is scheduled and the owner has named the legal seller. Before that there is nothing to sell. The first work is three repository-only PRs plus docs, and users see no change.

scores.design: A: friction (open by default, pay at cost by exception)
scores.reason: The best experience for people without a cloud account (one GitHub sign-in plus a $10 Apple Pay top-up, device code on pods), and its cost-based free line (12 cents or less per download) is the best rule. But it builds a payments business while nothing is for sale: 14 PRs, a legal seller, a merchant-of-record review, a ledger, refunds, support and GDPR work. Collecting money also brings the merchant's 'all necessary rights and licenses' attestation, which is hard for sources with no licence. Its mirror-first fetch quietly amends rule C8 (the committed URL is the only one fetch_data.py accepts), and its 10 GiB cap on free bytes served from GCS is too loose for $200. Criteria scores: friction 9, recovery 8, cost 7, effort 3, terms 7, fit 7.

scores.design: B: recovery (Google bills heavy users directly; we run no login or billing)
scores.reason: Winner. It is the least to build and run (about 5 to 7 PRs, mostly repository-only, with no money handled). Recovery is exactly Google's list price. Restricted or unchecked terms are open-only or a hard error, and it disturbs the data store least. Its correct calls: BigQuery in the US multi-region, a dedicated public project for BigQuery (a table's path exposes the project id), and the optional 'pay your own way' kill-switch mode. Weaknesses: a 64 MiB free line that contradicts its own research and would make the WorldPop 1 km grid a build error; no mirror by default; no route for people without a cloud account, triggered only by a demand count that undercounts. Criteria scores: friction 6, recovery 8, cost 7, effort 9, terms 9, fit 9.

scores.design: C: leverage (sponsors pay for free, users' clouds pay for paid)
scores.reason: The right way to scale the free tier (AWS Open Data, Google Public Datasets, Hugging Face, Zenodo). It is careful about licences, and its rule of keeping the GCS copy of a mirror-only object in the Requester Pays bucket is a good one. But its cost case depends on sponsor acceptance, which is discretionary, and on licence fixes covering most of the bytes: WorldPop is not_checked and is on 85.8% of the bytes; AFND has no licence and is on 89.2%. Its own 100x figure without sponsors is $596. BigQuery in us-east1 would block joins with bigquery-public-data, and multi-host fetching adds vendors and sync work. Criteria scores: friction 7, recovery 8, cost 6, effort 6, terms 9, fit 7.

keyClaims.claim: Anonymous requests to a Requester Pays bucket fail with 400 UserProjectMissing. The requester pays operations and egress, and the bucket owner always pays storage. So the free/paid line has to be a bucket boundary.

Buckets with Requester Pays disabled still accept requests that include a billing project, and the charges go to that project. So --billing-project works on the free bucket too (page last updated 2026-10-13).

The BigQuery sandbox needs no credit card or billing account, has a 1 TiB/month query limit, and expires tables after 60 days. Managed academic accounts must select an organization (page last updated 2026-10-15).
BigQuery bills queries on shared data to the querier, and 'The data owner is not charged'. On-demand queries cost $6.25/TiB after 1 TiB/month free, with a 10 MB minimum per table referenced.

In BigQuery, single-region locations don't match multi-region locations, so joining a us-east1 dataset with the US multi-region becomes a global query. Global queries need opt-in in both the querying and the data project, plus a permission only BigQuery Admin holds among predefined roles. So the Atlas dataset belongs in the US multi-region.
GCS internet egress is $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB, and Always Free gives 100 GB/month of egress from North America in us-east1. A full 0.25 GiB release costs about $0.03 to serve.

Stripe Managed Payments adds 3.5% per successful transaction to standard Stripe fees. Sellers must hold all necessary rights and licences to distribute the product, its information-services tax codes exclude data brokering, and it does not sell to buyers in China, among other restricted countries.
Paddle charges 5% + 50 cents per checkout transaction, with bespoke pricing for products under $10.
Stripe card fees are 2.9% + 30 cents, so a $10 top-up loses $0.59, and charging per download (about $0.03) is uncollectable.
ORCID's Public API may not be used 'in connection with any revenue-generating product or service', so ORCID is not used as a sign-in.
AWS Open Data covers S3 storage and outbound transfer. It requires data usable for any purpose, excludes licences that limit commercial use (CC BY-NC), and does not allow gated access.
Hugging Face downloads are free but rate-limited (3,000 resolver requests per 5 minutes per anonymous IP, 5,000 for a free user), and free public storage is best-effort.
DuckDB reads Hugging Face dataset files directly via hf:// paths, so heavy SQL over the mirror costs us nothing.
The education data transfer waiver covers internet egress up to 15% of monthly Google Cloud fees for Internet2 NET+, GEANT and reseller customers. It is not available to pay-as-you-go card customers.
For organizations created on or after 2024-05-03, domain-restricted sharing is enforced by default, which can block allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers grants unless custom policies add exceptions.

Release 2026-10-18 has 248 objects (271,494,507 bytes; the largest is 7,517,799 bytes). AFND is a source of 113 objects and 89.2% of the bytes; WorldPop (not_checked) of 62 objects and 85.8%; GeneReviews (non_commercial) of 6. data_release.py accepts any non-empty terms status, and the manifest uses restriction_found where commercial_use.py uses restricted.
The kill switch removes allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers from the data-store bucket only, at 150% of actual spend. The web bucket and the rest of the project keep billing.

Cost model: about $0-3/month now. At 100x users: about $186/month from GCS alone, about $49 with mirror-first fetching. At 100x users and data: about $338 without the mirror (over budget), about $68 with it. Requester Pays and BigQuery query costs land on users, not us.

checks.claim: Cost model: about $0-3/month now. At 100x users: about $186/month from GCS alone, about $49 with mirror-first fetching. At 100x users and data: about $338 without the mirror (over budget), about $68 with it. Requester Pays and BigQuery query costs land on users, not us.
checks.evidence: I recomputed every figure from the confirmed prices: $0.12/GiB, 93.13 GiB free, $0.02 per GiB-month storage, $0.023 BigQuery storage over 10 GiB. Now: 21.4 GiB, inside the free allowance ($2.57 if billed). 100x GCS only: 1,548.7 GiB → $185.85. 100x mirror first: 410.9 GiB → $49.31. 100x users and data, GCS only: 2,784.5 GiB → $334.14, plus $0.10 + $2.99 + $0.92 + $0.04 = $338.19. With the mirror: 534.5 GiB → $64.14, total $68.19. Bulk storage of 149.5 GiB is $2.99 Standard and $0.60 Coldline. BigQuery storage of 40 billable GiB is $0.92. Both buckets are in us-east1 (provision_data_store_bucket.py and provision_atlas_web_bucket.py, LOCATION = 'us-east1'), so Always Free applies. Who pays: Requester Pays and BigQuery 'data owner is not charged' are confirmed above. Caveats, all about assumptions rather than prices: (1) Always Free is per billing account; (2) CI --verify-remote stays at 5.1 GiB in the 100x-data column even though the release grows; (3) all traffic figures are assumed, as the doc says.

checks.claim: (§5) An 11% margin (price = list ÷ 0.89) 'covers the worst merchant-of-record fee on a $10 top-up' (Paddle $1.00; Stripe Managed Payments about $0.94).
checks.evidence: The domestic-card figures are right: Paddle 5% + 50¢ = $1.00, and Stripe Managed Payments 2.9% + 30¢ + 3.5% = $0.94. But Managed Payments adds 3.5% 'to your standard Stripe processing fees', and those fees include '+ 1.5% for international cards' and '+ 1% if currency conversion is required'. For a foreign buyer paying in another currency, the $10 top-up costs $0.29 + $0.15 + $0.10 + $0.30 + $0.35 = $1.19, more than the $1.10 the margin raises. The 11% is not the worst case for Managed Payments; it covers it only for domestic cards.

checks.claim: (§6.2) For the 42 GiB example (about $5.04 at list price), the Phase 3 quote is 'Quote $5.69', leaving a balance of $5.31.
checks.evidence: This is arithmetic, not a pricing claim. 42 GiB × $0.12 ÷ 0.89 = $5.66 (or $5.67 at the rounded $0.135/GiB), not $5.69. With a $1 allowance the shortfall is about $4.66, and $10 − $4.66 leaves a balance of about $5.34, not $5.31.

Cloud Storage and BigQuery are not eligible, so for GCS egress the kill switch remains the only brake. A Phase 3 broker on Cloud Run could use a native spend cap.
